#### Open Issues

The increasing use of AI in the Fintech sector is well documented in the literature, highlighting the growing prevalence of these technologies across the financial industry. At the same time, interest in green Fintech – technology’s role in promoting sustainable practices in finance – is gaining traction both in academia and in industry. However, while current studies primarily focus on how technology can support financial institutions in meeting environmental and sustainability requirements, there is a lack of research examining the carbon footprint associated with the use of AI itself, particularly in computationally intensive contexts like Fintech.

Existing literature shows a significant gap regarding decarbonization techniques specifically applied to AI in the financial context. While current studies largely focus on the direct impacts of digital technologies in supporting the green transition of financial products and services, they overlook the implicit environmental cost of deploying such technologies. This is especially critical in financial organizations, where the demand for timely execution, technical efficiency, and regulatory compliance is high. This oversight has led to a slow adoption of Green AI practices within Fintech, where Green AI refers to strategies aimed at reducing the carbon impact of AI models employed in the financial sector.

Financial institutions and organizations could greatly benefit from implementing Green AI techniques, yet face unique challenges such as the time-sensitive nature of use cases, technical and infrastructural constraints, financial implications, internal resistance, and the regulatory compliance issues inherent in a highly regulated sector. The primary reason for the lack of adoption lies in the absence of a comprehensive work in the literature that aggregates, critically analyzes, and adapts these techniques in light of these specific constraints. This causes also a lack of documented case studies that could encourage other financial firms in their path toward the decarbonization of their AIs

This book chapter seeks to address this research gap by providing a critical and systematic analysis of Green AI techniques applicable to Fintech, examining their potential and limitations within the sector’s unique framework.

### 4\. DECARBONIZING THE AI TRAINING PHASE IN THE FINANCIAL DOMAIN

In this section we are going to explore some of the techniques that has been presented in the literature for the mitigation of the carbon footprint of the AI training phase. Compared with a traditional software engineering project, the training phase of an AI project corresponds to the development of the system, while the inference phase corresponds to the system itself going in production. While the emissions of an AI model going in production are somewhat expected just like every software engineering project, the emissions caused by the development of the project – i.e. the training of the model – are new. In fact, training an AI model replaces the work of developers, who usually code the business logic in a top-down fashion: requirements are elicited, then they become use cases which are implemented after defining the main relationships among the data. This requires a high knowledge on the domain, but most of the rules governing a phenomenon could be hard to elicit even for domain experts. Moreover, the relations among the data may change over time. Training an AI can be seen as a “brute force approach” to bypass all the traditional steps of software development, since it does not require knowledge on the domain nor to formalize the relationships among the data: they are just extracted from the evidence, in a bottom-up (or data-driven) approach. Such brute force approach to software development consumes way more energy, since it requires to calibrate the weight of billions of parameters of neural networks. Some algorithms may be more efficient and can converge in less time, but the energy computation required will be always more than the energy needed by a developer coding the system rules within his or her development environment.

It is also valid in the Fintech domain, for instance let’s consider the SCA (Strong Customer Authentication) exemption case. The Payment Service Directive 2 (PSD2) allows to bypass the Two Factor Authentication (2FA) for digital payments if the card issuer performs a Transaction Risk Analysis (TRA). The normative does not enforce the way the TRA should be performed: the decision to bypass the SCA/2FA could come after either a top-down or a bottom-up evaluation. A top-down evaluation is currently the norm, for instance: a web site (or an IP address) can be blacklisted; a whole country can be blacklisted; a payment card could have been recently issued and there is not enough information on the customer; the payment amount is high and bypassing SCA is just too risky. These are just a few examples of some top-down rules that the domain expert could configure within the TRA software. A bottom-up approach instead will look directly into the data – i.e. the history of fraudulent transaction – to extract relations among the features to reconstruct the shapes of the typical fraudulent (or non-fraudulent) transactions. With AI, even the relations that are not visible to domain experts (because they are too complicated or not close to human understanding or way of thinking) emerge. By the way, brute-forcing such relations by training some AI is way more energy consuming than the one required by a domain expert inputting well known rules in a software component. For this reason, training an AI in the financial domain will always consume more energy than configuring a traditional non-AI system.

In the next sections we will see how the demand shifting and demand shaping strategies can be applied in the financial domain to mitigate the carbon footprint of training AI.

#### Flexible Start

Flexible Start (FS) is a kind of temporal demand shifting strategy applied to the case of AI training. Its working principle is very simple: just wait for better Carbon Intensity before starting to train. Its benefits have been measured for the first time in [Dodge et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor140) for 11 NLP and Computer vision tasks. A confirmation study ([Vergallo & Mainetti, 2024](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor183)) confirmed the gain in carbon saving for four Anomaly Detection (AD) tasks in the Fintech domain (fraud detection). For each training task [Dodge et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor140) calculated the operational emissions using GPUs' energy consumption tracked each 5 minutes, and historical MOER supplied by WattTime with a 5-minute granularity. It means that, in order to achieve the best results, it is not enough just to look at the Carbon Intensity in a specific moment, instead FS needs the forecasted values in a certain time window. In this way, the optimal starting time can be found, because just looking at the instantaneous Carbon Intensity may ignore subsequent fluctuations. Before reporting the results observed by [Dodge et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor140), it must be underlined that the maximum time window elongation for completing the 11 tasks is defined in two ways: a flat 24h increase for every task, and a relative 100% increase with respect to the original task duration. The relative time elongation is fairer, since longer tasks – like training a 6.1 billion parameter transformer – will have less advantage from FS if the time elongation is fixed (i.e., there are less options to span inside the time window). The carbon savings in this case are 3-7%, with smaller tasks achieving better results, because longer tasks have more probability to encounter moments of high Carbon Intensity during the training (because in FS when a training start, it does not stop until it ends). Just adding 24 hours, shorter tasks achieve very interesting results (26.8% for a 20-minute task). [Vergallo & Mainetti (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor183) replicated the experiment in the Fintech domain: the case of AD tasks. Four algorithms were benchmarked: Isolation Forest (IF) (Liu, F. T., 2008), Support Vector Machine (SVM) (Hearst, M. A., 1998), Autoencoder (AE) (Bank, D., 2023), and Hands-Free Strong Costumer Authentication (HF-SCA) ([Distante et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor139)). Carbon emissions baseline spans from 0.25kgCO2eq for SVM to 1.7kgCO2eq for HF-SCA. The algorithms were trained with the same dataset: a 5 million records transaction history provided by an Italian bank. The dataset is labelled, meaning that there’s Boolean fraud information for each transaction. Before commenting on the results of FS for the benchmarked algorithms, authors discuss the trade-off between carbon emissions and performance. Just looking at the performance metrics (in AD, the AUC score is considered), a decision maker may be tempted to choose HF-SCA because of its 97% score. Unfortunately, HF-SCA is also the most polluting choice, as seen above. AE has also good results (73%) with just 0.3 kgCO2eq, but the difference in the score is just too high to prefer AE. The decision maker could choose HF-SCA while opting for some carbon aware strategies like FS or the ones that will be presented in the next subsections. Another question that could drive the algorithm decision would be: how often should the algorithm be retrained? This will also be discussed in the next subsections.

#### Pause and Resume

It is a bit more elaborated strategy, since Pause & Resume (PaR) starts at time zero and – as its name suggests – look continuously at the Carbon Intensity signal to determine non-computation periods, i.e. periods in which the training workload should be momentarily stopped. The reference works for PaR are again [Dodge et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor140) and [Vergallo & Mainetti (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor183), hence the experiments’ setup is the same as in the previous subsection. The observations reported better results for longer workloads: up to 11.4% in [Dodge et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor140), and up to 7.3% in [Vergallo & Mainetti (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor183) (in the latter, workloads are shorter). It is intuitively correct, as with PaR longer workloads can pause their execution during moments of high Carbon Intensity. In the case of longer workloads (e.g. ML, computer vision, NLP) PaR is a preferable strategy. With PaR, the Fintech stakeholders could significantly decarbonize the impact of their AI just adopting a quite straightforward rule.

#### Follow the Sun

FS and PaR use temporal demand shifting to mitigate the impact of training AI algorithms. Nevertheless, their benefits highly depend on the region where the workloads are launched, because of the mix of energy sources characterizing the specific region. A further step may include a wise selection of the Cloud region where the computations would be performed. Both [Dodge et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor140) and [Vergallo & Mainetti (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor183) provide useful visual representation of the different carbon footprints of training the same algorithms across several Cloud regions.

However, if all of us trained our AI in France or in Northern Europe, those regions risk running out of clean/green energy very fast. A dynamic approach is mandatory to make regional selection more sustainable. As the name itself (partially) suggests, Follow the Sun (FtS) moves the computation workloads across different Cloud regions. Like a sunflower, the strategy looks continuously for a region with lower Carbon Intensity, and when it finds one, it stops the execution and moves the semi-finished model to the new region. Despite its name, FtS takes into account all the available renewable sources. In pre-print work, Vergallo et al. (2024) report a 14.58% carbon saving for four AD algorithms using FtS.

Nevertheless, the drawbacks of FtS should be considered. Despite the feasibility of such an architecture have been proved ([James & Schien, 2019](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor153)), the increased architectural complexity with respect to FS and PaR is evident. Moreover, not every AI workload can be dumped. Finally, a major source of problem is the data transfer towards foreign countries. In fact, FtS does not comply with local regulations such as the European GDPR when datasets are moved in non-EU countries. However, Carbon Intensity can vary a lot also remaining in the same continent. Specifically talking about Fintech, without a very precise monitoring system for FtS, banks may fail in saying which server owns specific data.

By the way, FtS is a very interesting strategy, with proved efficacy, that could inspire a better management of workloads in distributed architectures.

#### Responsible Re-Train

The development of AI algorithm requires a training phase in which the algorithm learns from the data by identifying patterns and relationships. For instance, an AI for profiling user habits or AD needs data such as transactions performed by the individual user. The size of data grows over time, and this can lead to vulnerabilities related to changes in data distribution ([Lyu et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor166)). If user spending habits change over time, the AI model will need to be retrained to ensure high performance. These changes are called concept drift (Gama el al., 2014). The notion of concept drift in AI and ML is closely related to environmental sustainability. As already mentioned, training an AI requires significant computational and energy resources. If a company wants to remain competitive and offer AI-based tools to its customers, sooner or later it will have to update and improve its models to ensure high performance and thus release new CO2 into the atmosphere. However, it is possible to mitigate concept drift responsibly in order to reduce the CO2 emissions, such as by identifying the best time to replace an AI model with a more performing one, retraining the existing model only on the most recent data and discarding the most useless data, retraining the model only when one realizes a drop in performance.

The research of [Poenaru-Olaru et al. (2023a)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor173) was conducted with ING Nederland and is therefore of particular interest for the Fintech sector. The paper explored concept drift adaptation techniques and defined a new research path based on sustainability point of view. The three main concept drift adaptation techniques presented into the previously cited paper are: Dataset Adaptation, Model Adaptation and Frequency Adaptation ([Celik & Vanschoren, 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor133); [Gama et al.,2014](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor144); [Kavikondala et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor156)).

Dataset Adaptation techniques differ based on the time interval of the data to be considered for training. Periodically enlarging the training set ([Kavikondala et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor156)) involves the continuous addition of new data samples to the existing training set over time. Once a threshold is reached, the model is retrained using the extended dataset. Gradual forgetting assumes that most recent data are more relevant. For this reason, in the training phase, the assignment of weights takes into account the chronological order of samples. Abrupt forgetting involves training the model only on new data – older samples are removed.

Model Adaptation focuses on the performance of the model. In this context, a model can be replaced by one that performs better and is appropriate for performing the specific task; or it can be retrained using a new or more up-to-date dataset.

The Frequency Adaptation consists of improving the model using newly available data. This process can occur periodically (e.g. every month, every six months, etc.) without any investigation (blind adaptation) or only when needed (informed adaptation) ([Gama et al., 2014](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor144)). Each technique can be addressed with environmental sustainability in mind. The lowest-impact approach for Dataset Adaptation is the abrupt forgetting - only the most recent samples of dataset are used to retrain the AI model. [Verdecchia et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor180) examines the impact of different training dataset sizes on energy efficiency and concluded that small datasets require little energy during training. Among the Model Adaptation techniques, it is not yet clear whether it is convenient to retrain a model on new data or to choose a new one - by retracing the steps of exploring, analyzing, and testing the architecture described in the previous paragraphs. From a Frequency Adaptation perspective, [Poenaru-Olaru et al. (2023a)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor173) concluded that the model adaptation should be done only when necessary, even though practitioners adapt models on a periodic basis without investigating the need for adaptation ([Lyu et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor166)).

Monitoring the concept drift becomes crucial in Fintech to develop AI algorithms that can maintain performance over time. If an AD algorithm were not updated with the user's new spending habits, it might fail to notice abnormal payments - causing harm to the user and a loss of trust in the bank - or generate false alarms, blocking an intentional user transaction, and thus causing a bad user experience (UX). [Poenaru-Olaru et al. (2023b)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor172) studied the application of a tool called the concept drift detector, applied to state-of-the-art AD algorithms, such as the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), Spectral Residuals (SR), Prediction Confidence Interval (PCI), Long Short-Term Memory Autoencoder (LSTM-AE), and Spectral Residuals Convolutional Neural Networks (SR-CNN), using different retraining techniques. The concept drift detector makes it possible to analyze data time series and identify when a model needs to be retrained to ensure high performance. This tool has a crucial role in avoiding both excessive model retraining - with wasted energy and increased carbon footprint - and too infrequent retraining, which would cause reduced performance. However, existing literature does not report quantitative evidence on how much carbon is saved using one re-train strategy or another. Therefore, the Fintech industry should try the presented techniques, monitor and recalibrate the approach.

### 5\. DECARBONIZING THE AI INFERENCE PHASE IN THE FINANCIAL DOMAIN

The carbon emissions caused by inferencing (i.e. by an AI model working on data it has never seen before) may conceptually correspond to the emission of a traditional software system going in production. However, several considerations can be done. First, the Rebound effect (Willenbacher, 2021): groundbreaking technologies like AI not only make processes and companies more efficient, but they also create new needs. For example, people use ChatGPT to write texts in minutes instead of hours, but actually they also create content they would have not written, just because ChatGPT is available. This effect happens several times in various domains: a more efficient engine makes people travel more, batteries with higher capacities allow people to stream video on social networks all over the day, a faster GPU allow to train more AI, etc.

Also in Fintech, the Rebound effect makes the benefits of advanced technologies like AI, ML, and data analytics partially offset, leadings to unintended increases in overall energy consumption or emissions. AI and ML models are increasingly used for complex financial risk analysis, fraud detection, and customer personalization. While these technologies improve operational efficiency, their implementation requires substantial computational power, potentially leading to higher carbon emissions despite the promise of efficiency. For example, AI and ML-based automated trading platforms require vast computational resources to run real-time analysis of markets and execute high-frequency trades. As these platforms expand and more market participants use algorithmic trading, the cumulative computational load increases. Despite the efficiency of automated trades, the need for continuous data processing and low-latency systems increases energy consumption across data centers and financial networks. Moreover, as more Fintech services integrate AI and ML, banks and financial institutions must upgrade their hardware infrastructure to handle the increased computational load. This often means adopting new systems based on GPUs, which are designed for high-performance computing tasks. However, the production of these GPUs carries an “embedded carbon” footprint – referring to the carbon emissions generated during the manufacturing, transportation and disposal processes. The need for this advanced hardware increases both direct energy consumption and the indirect carbon impact, further intensifying the rebound effect.

The Rebound effect cannot be avoided, so the carbon emissions of the inference phase of an AI model will tend to be higher than the ones of the production phase of traditional software engineering system. What can be done to decarbonize the inference phase? The Fintech world has some options that are discussed in the next subsections.

#### Model Compression

One of the challenges facing Fintech companies is making AI models usable by their customers. Complex ML and DL models require a high computational cost and a large amount of available memory ([Schwartz et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor176); [Desislavov et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor137)). This makes the large models not usable on consumer smartphones or IoT devices ([Zhu & Gupta, 2017](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor193)) where processing power, battery life, storage capacity can be a bottleneck. To address these challenges, model compression techniques can help solve the problem by simplifying the model.

Model compression is a set of ML and DL technique to reducing the size and complexity of AI model, making them more accessible and usable for deployment on constrained devices. Moreover, compressed model could also replace the original ones in the Cloud, hence mitigating the carbon footprint of the inference phase. Three main categories of model compression exist: quantization, pruning and distillation.

#### Model Quantization

Weights in AI algorithm are numerical parameters referring to the importance of individual inputs. Typically, they are represented by a 32-bit single-precision floating format (FP32). As shown in [Figure 4](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor112), model quantization technique involves reducing the precision of the parameters using a 4-bit or 8-bit integer format (INT8) ([Gholami et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor145)). There are two main categories of model quantization. The first focuses on how the ranges of parameters are mapped; the second focused on when these ranges are calculated. The first category includes uniform quantization, non-uniform quantization and mixed-precision quantization. The second category includes static quantization, dynamic quantization, and quantization-aware training.

#### Figure 4. Example of a weight matrix in FP32 being mapped to INT8

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f04](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f04.png)

Uniform quantization is a technique where the range of parameter values is divided into equally spaced intervals, and each interval is mapped to the nearest quantization level. This approach can be divided into scalar quantization and vector quantization. Scalar quantization refers to mapping each parameter independently of the others; vector quantization refers to mapping groups of parameters jointly. Scalar quantization ([Choi et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor136)) can be computationally efficient but is less efficient in terms of data compression; vector quantization ([Wu & Yu, 2019](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor188)) preserves performance better but increases model complexity.

Unlike uniform quantization in which the intervals are equally spaced, in non-uniform quantization, the parameters are mapped into variable-length intervals. The size of intervals depends on the density of parameters. Small intervals will be assigned to denser parameter ranges. In [Figure 5](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor113), real values, represented by orange markers, on r-axis are mapped to discrete, lower precision values in the quantized domain (Q-axis). In uniform quantization, the spacing between these quantized values is regular, while in non-uniform quantization, the distances between levels can be not regular. Non-uniform quantization improves compression efficiency but increases the computation cost. One popular non-uniform quantization technique is k-means quantization ([Choi et al., 2016](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor135)).

#### Figure 5. Comparison between uniform quantization (a) and non-uniform quantization (b)

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f05](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f05.png)

Mixed-precision quantization assigns different representations depending on the importance of the parameter. The most important model’s parameters will be quantified using more bits to maintain performance while less important parameters will be represented with fewer bits to reduce model’s size. Like uniform vector quantization, parameters can be grouped together before being quantized but it is also possible to grouped layers ([Dong et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor141); [Pandey et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor170)).

Static quantization is a post-training method in which the intervals are pre-calculated and remain fixed during inference phase. This technique is computationally efficient but may result in lower accuracy. Dynamic quantization involves not just converting weights but also activation in real-time^(35). This technique is computationally expensive but often achieves the highest accuracy. However, practitioners prefer to use static quantization ([Gholami et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor145)). Thus, the quantization approaches seen so far involve changing parameters before, after or during model training. Instead, a technique that incorporates the quantization process is quantization-aware training. In quantization-aware training procedure ([Figure 6](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor114)), forward pass simulates low-precision behavior (weights are quantized with fewer bits), backward pass remains the same. Forward pass is the process where input data is passed through the network to compute an output; backward pass – or back propagation – is the process of updating the network’s parameters and weights based on the error between the output and the true value ([Gurney, 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor149); [Wythoff, 1993](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor189)).

#### Figure 6. Example of quantization-aware training process

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f06](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f06.png)

#### Model Pruning

Model pruning is a technique aims to reduce the size of ML and DL algorithms by removing redundant or less important parameters. For instance, the type of device used may not bring useful information to an AI algorithm for profiling user habits. This implies that parameter and related connections between network nodes might be removed. A pruning process can be unstructured or structured; one-shot or iterative.

Unstructured pruning involves the removal of weights or connections based on a threshold or ranking criteria ([Figure 7](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor115)). This method allows a fine-grained compression, but it may result in irregular data access patterns, which are harder to optimize with hardware acceleration. The most common unstructured pruning including magnitude pruning ([Han et al., 2015](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor150)), gradient pruning ([Liu et al., 2014](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor163); [Liu & Wu, 2019](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor162)), hessian pruning ([Liu et al. 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor164)).

#### Figure 7. Example of unstructured weight pruning. a) is the initial network; b) is the selection of weights to be removed. The blue weights are those that have been selected to be removed; c) is the final compressed network after the unstructured pruning process

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f07](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f07.png)

Structured pruning focused on removing neurons, filters or entire layers, rather than individual weights. In [Figure 8, a](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor116)) is the initial network; b) is the selection of weights and neurons to be removed. The blue items are those that have been selected to be removed; c) is the final compressed network after the structured pruning process.

In this approach data layout is preserved, allowing the hardware acceleration. However, removing entire filters or layers can lead to a decrease in model performance, as a larger sections or important parameters are removed. The most common structured pruning including filter pruning ([Lin et al. 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor161)), channel pruning ([Liu & Wu, 2019](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor162)), layer pruning ([Chen & Zhao., 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor134)).

#### Figure 8. Example of structured weight and neurons pruning

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f08](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f08.png)

One-shot pruning ([Chen & Zhao, 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor134)) involves a single pruning step where weights, filters, or neurons are removed. This method is computationally efficient, but it often leads to a drop of initial performance. Iterative pruning ([Castellano et al., 1997](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor132); [Gordienko et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor146)) involves multiple pruning steps, where weights, filters, or neurons are gradually removed. After each pruning step, the model is retrained, allowing it to gradually adapt. This approach often preserve performance but leads at a higher computational cost.

#### Knowledge Distillation

Knowledge distillation is a technique aim to transfer knowledge from a large, complex and pre-trained model (teacher model) to a smaller and simple one (student model). The goal is to train the simplest model so that it behaves like the complex model. The training of the student model is based on the original data and outputs provided by the teacher model, with which knowledge transfer takes place ([Figure 9](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor117)).

#### Figure 9. Example of knowledge distillation process. The student model tries to mimic the behavior of the teacher by going to correct the parameters of interest

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f09](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f09.png)

In this context, knowledge refers to the information captured by the teacher model and transferred to the student model. Instead, distillation refers to training algorithms for both teacher and student models. It is the strategy used to guide the transfer of knowledge from the teacher model. [Gou et al. (2021)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor147) have led a survey about knowledge distillation strategies. Knowledge can be grouped in response-based, feature-based and relation-based. Instead, distillation can be grouped in offline, online and self-distillation. In response-based knowledge, the student model is trained to mimic the final prediction of the teacher model using logits ([Figure 10](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor118)). In feature-based knowledge, intermediate feature or activations are transferred from the teacher model to the student model. In this case, the student model learns from the intermediate layers as well as the final layer as in the case of the response-based knowledge ([Figure 11](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor119)). In relation-based knowledge, the student model learns from the teacher how samples relate to each other. This approach helps the student model to better understand the data structure ([Figure 12](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor120)).

#### Figure 10. Example of response-based knowledge distillation

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f10](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f10.png)

#### Figure 11. Example of feature-based knowledge distillation

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f11](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f11.png)

#### Figure 12. Example of relation-based knowledge distillation

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f12](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f12.png)

Offline or vanilla knowledge distillation consist of two phases. The first is the training of large teacher model. In the second phase, student model is trained using the knowledge (logits or features) from the teacher model. This approach requires an additional time component because the training of both models cannot occur simultaneously. Moreover, a performance gap between teacher and the student remains wide. In online knowledge distillation, teacher model and student model are trained simultaneously. This involves the possibility of using deep mutual learning techniques ([Zhang et al., 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor191)), in which different neural networks collaborate with each other to transfer knowledge. In self-distillation, the same network is used for teacher and student model. In this approach, the model learns from its output improving the generalization capability without external guidance. Self-distillation offers improvements in accuracy, hardware acceleration, and model compression over conventional knowledge distillation ([Zhang et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor190)). All of these three techniques are shown in [Figure 13](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor121).

#### Figure 13. Comparison between distillation techniques

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f13](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch002.f13.png)

#### Deferred and Relocated Inference: Challenges and Limitations

Model compression represents a form of demand shaping, i.e. a strategy to request less features from a system without compromising its long-term value. In this case, the features are the computation capability of a processor, and the related memory demand. However, temporal and spatial demand shifting may represent an option also for the inference phase, particularly:

*   • Temporal demand shifting is a kind of deferred inference, meaning that the AI’s end users (i.e. the user that take advantage of the features of an AI model deployed in production) can receive a suggestion about waiting a certain amount of time before querying the AI, in order to take advantage of better Carbon Intensity.
    
*   • Spatial demand shifting can relocate the inference task to the geographical region with better Carbon Intensity. However, the carbon footprint of a set of multiple servers up and running should be taken into account.
    

Research in this area has not yet provided interesting evidence. Moreover, the peculiarities of the Fintech domain deserve specific research efforts. For example, the banking domain has some time-sensitivity requirements that makes it cumbersome to postpone computation to match better Carbon Intensity. The case of real time monitoring of transactions for fraud prevention is particularly illustrative, as delays in detecting fraudulent activity could result in significant financial losses. In such scenarios, immediate responses are critical, and any postponement in computation to optimize for Carbon Intensity could compromise the system's security and reliability. Therefore, solutions in the Fintech sector must carefully balance environmental sustainability goals with the need for swift and accurate processing.

The research challenge lies in finding a trade-off between time-sensitivity in fraud detection and the goal of reducing carbon emissions. In the context of banking, where timely fraud detection is crucial, banks might consider accepting a certain percentage of frauds that are not detected immediately in order to reduce their carbon footprint. This compromise raises important questions about the balance between financial security and environmental sustainability.

One possible approach (Strategy 1) is to wait for the Carbon Intensity of the energy grid to drop below a specific threshold before performing fraud detection inference. This method could reduce carbon emissions by relying on cleaner energy sources. However, the trade-off here is the delay in detecting fraud, potentially allowing malicious transactions to proceed undetected for a longer period. The relationship between fraud detection delays and CO2 savings could be represented in a graph, showing how increasing the amount of CO2 saved results in a higher number of frauds that are not detected in a timely manner. Additionally, a third dimension of the graph could model the economic damage caused by subsequent fraudulent transactions that occur before the compromised payment instrument is blocked. This would depend on the specific behavior of fraudsters in the dataset and may vary significantly across different datasets.

Another approach (Strategy 2) addresses the time-sensitivity issue more directly: instead of delaying computation, the bank can shift the fraud detection task to servers in regions where CI is lower at the time of inference. This meets the real-time requirement but comes at the cost of extra carbon emissions associated with the embodied carbon of additional servers and increased networking overhead. It also introduces a higher infrastructure burden. Despite these added carbon costs, this strategy maintains the integrity of fraud detection without compromising on response times. By running computations on cleaner energy grids without delaying the process, Strategy 2 offers a more practical solution to time-sensitive fraud detection, although with potential hidden carbon costs.

Comparing the two strategies, the carbon saving of Strategy 2 can be simply computed by offloading tasks to cleaner grids while maintaining real-time responses. For Strategy 1, research provides insights through a graph relating the number of frauds not detected in real-time to the kilograms of CO2 saved, revealing a clear trade-off between fraud detection performance and environmental impact. Furthermore, applying both strategies to compressed and uncompressed ML models would offer additional nuance. In can be expected that using compressed models (which are faster and more efficient) would allow more frauds to be detected in real-time while achieving the same carbon savings, compared to uncompressed models.

Finally, an interesting dimension of the research would involve comparing the marginal operating emission rate (MOER) from different cities. This would show that fraud detection performance is inherently better in regions where the energy grid is cleaner, potentially providing a natural advantage for financial institutions operating in those areas. The results of these strategies will not only benefit fraud detection but can also extend to other time-sensitive domains, such as cybersecurity and emergency response systems, where real-time processing is critical and must be balanced with carbon reduction efforts.

### 7\. DISCUSSION

In this section, we critically evaluate the limitations of AI decarbonization techniques and discuss the challenges that face both the Fintech industry and the research community. These challenges span regulatory, financial, technical, and organizational domains, illustrating the significant gap between theoretical advances in Green AI and practical implementation in financial services.

One major regulatory challenge concerns data privacy laws that limit the potential for using spatial and temporal variability in carbon intensity to optimize AI workloads. Techniques that leverage spatial variability to execute tasks in regions with cleaner energy sources often conflict with privacy regulations that restrict the geographic transfer of sensitive data. Similarly, while techniques exploiting temporal variability – such as running AI tasks during periods of lower carbon intensity – are promising, they may not be feasible for time-sensitive financial operations, like high-frequency trading or fraud detection, where even minimal delays can translate into substantial financial risks.

From a technical standpoint, while a growing number of tools and methods for Green AI are available, they are not yet designed for easy, out-of-the-box implementation. This gap is compounded by a shortage of specialized “green” developers familiar with sustainability practices. Many developers accustomed to abundant cloud resources may not prioritize energy optimization, leading to resource-heavy practices that overlook efficiency. Smaller banks face additional limitations, as they frequently outsource software and lack control over infrastructure, reducing their ability to implement sustainable practices internally.

Organizational resistance further complicates the integration of Green AI. For many financial institutions, technical sustainability does not appear urgent. Banks often address ESG concerns through investments, customer selection, or by purchasing renewable energy, leading to a perception that these measures are sufficient. Green AI, by contrast, is sometimes perceived as risky or as a potential compromise to performance or regulatory compliance, creating additional hesitancy to adopt these techniques.

A key finding of this assessment is that while Green AI in Fintech has received theoretical attention, it primarily focuses on technology-for-sustainability rather than on sustainable practices for AI itself. Despite the growing number of proposed decarbonization techniques, the field lacks empirical studies, especially within the financial sector. Many techniques require advanced skills, hardware, and resources for customization and experimentation that not all institutions can readily access. Moreover, engaging bank customers in Green AI practices could foster awareness and buy-in, making them crucial allies in this transition.

The findings from this analysis raise important questions for the industry and research community. Given the difficulties in changing established practices, particularly in large institutions, we must consider whether smaller actors in the banking ecosystem – such as startup accelerators – could drive sustainable practices more flexibly and rapidly. Additionally, collaborations between banks and energy providers could provide access to more granular carbon data than is available through public sources, enabling optimized energy use and cost savings. Regulatory authorities like central banks may have a crucial role in establishing standards for Green AI in Fintech. Should each institution be required to conduct Green AI experiments to gather data before enforcing industry standards? Setting baseline sustainability requirements, perhaps mandating a minimum of one Green AI experiment per organization, would allow financial institutions to assess their results before any broader mandates take effect.

This raises another question about timing and suitability: When should these techniques be considered, and when might they be impractical? Building new services with sustainable principles from the outset is far more feasible than retrofitting existing systems. Legacy products often require complex refactoring, while smaller-scale, non-critical services present an easier entry point, potentially raising awareness among developers and managers about the value of green practices. To make Green AI a reality in Fintech, there must first be dashboards and metrics that provide clear, quantifiable measures of an AI system’s carbon footprint. Standardized metrics, such as grams of CO2eq per customer, per transaction, per fraud detection, or per investment, could allow institutions to set concrete sustainability targets. Additional data signals, like the financial cost of not executing AI due to carbon intensity constraints, could support more precise scheduling and location choices for energy-intensive AI tasks.

Developers and AI scientists will have essential roles in this transition. Developers can facilitate the adoption of Green AI by creating solutions such as automated compression tools, energy tracking software, low-energy encryption, and SDKs that preserve privacy and meet the unique needs of Fintech. AI scientists, meanwhile, can advance Green AI practices by broadening their focus beyond model accuracy to include efficiency and resource optimization. By evaluating the energy, time, and computational costs associated with model training and deployment, researchers can help reduce the environmental footprint of AI models used in Fintech. AI scientists can further contribute by prioritizing model reuse and task-specific fine-tuning, as well as by selecting smaller models that meet the needs of specific Fintech applications. This shift in focus could limit the use of “Red AI” – those models with excessive resource demands – by selecting approaches that reduce computational overhead without compromising essential outcomes.

Reorienting AI workloads to align with sustainable practices presents a unique challenge, especially in the finance sector, which is driven by opportunistic goals and profitability. Financial institutions thrive on the ability to act swiftly in response to investment opportunities and minimize losses associated with risks like fraud or market volatility. However, it remains an open question whether the opportunistic nature of these workloads can be adjusted to prioritize sustainability. Viewing the planet as a stakeholder would mean considering long-term environmental impacts, investing in initiatives that respect ecological boundaries, and making decisions that may not yield immediate financial returns. This question challenges the profit-driven approach embedded in the financial sector and raises concerns about whether these values are compatible with a Green AI vision. Indeed, the broader context of capitalism and its role in contributing to environmental challenges cannot be ignored in this conversation.

### 8\. CONCLUSION

The transition from Fintech to Green Fintech is both a necessary and complex journey, driven by the urgent need to align AI systems with the sustainability goals of financial institutions. As AI techniques, particularly Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), become integral to the financial sector, their energy consumption and carbon footprint cannot be ignored. This chapter has explored the landscape of Green AI techniques, focusing on how they can be applied to the Fintech domain, which presents specific challenges such as time-sensitive operations, strict regulatory requirements, and data protection needs.

The main results of this chapter can be summarized as follows:

*   • A centralized resource has been established to guide the Fintech sector in adopting AI decarbonization techniques, providing an accessible foundation for sustainable AI integration across the industry.
    
*   • An extensive and in-depth review of green Fintech and green AI is presented, encompassing the latest advancements and setting the groundwork for further innovation and research in sustainable technology.
    
*   • Relevant standards and initiatives for environmental sustainability within organizations are systematically outlined, giving Fintech companies a clear framework to understand and implement these practices.
    
*   • Current case studies in green Fintech have been collected and analyzed, with significant gaps identified, highlighting areas that call for new insights and actionable strategies.
    
*   • A detailed examination of decarbonization techniques for both the training and deployment of AI is provided, with each method critically analyzed against the particular demands and constraints of the Fintech industry.
    
*   • The discussion delves into the unique regulatory, performance, and operational constraints Fintech faces, illuminating the complex interplay between green AI strategies and the sector’s specific requirements.
    

Future research directions must address the significant gaps in empirical evidence for Green AI techniques within Fintech. To assess the applicability of these techniques and gain regulatory support, industry-specific case studies and data collection are essential. Only through rigorous testing and validation will we be able to measure the effectiveness of Green AI practices in Fintech and determine the suitability of these approaches for diverse financial applications.

This work is intended to be useful for the following stakeholders:

*   • Financial institutions (banks, Fintech companies, and asset managers): The insights provided can help these institutions reduce the carbon footprint of their AI-driven products and services. By adopting Green AI techniques, they can align with sustainability goals, reduce energy costs, and demonstrate their commitment to environmental responsibility without compromising on the speed or accuracy of financial operations.
    
*   • Regulatory bodies and supervisory authorities: The study offers valuable information for regulators who aim to encourage or mandate sustainable practices within the financial sector. It highlights how Green AI techniques can be integrated while maintaining compliance with legal requirements, particularly in areas of data protection, security, and fraud prevention, helping shape future policies.
    
*   • Practitioners (AI engineers, data scientists, and Fintech developers): Practitioners can directly apply the strategies and techniques discussed in this work to optimize the efficiency of AI systems. This includes improving energy efficiency during both training and inference phases of AI development, enabling the creation of more sustainable Fintech solutions that meet industry standards for performance.
    
*   • Students: This work provides students with an accessible introduction to the intersection of AI and sustainability in the financial sector. It serves as a valuable resource for understanding the importance of reducing AI's carbon footprint and offers practical insights into how sustainable AI practices can be applied in Fintech.
    
*   • Researchers: Researchers will find this work a useful foundation for further exploration of Green AI in the financial domain. It highlights areas where more investigation is needed, such as optimizing the trade-offs between performance and sustainability, and offers a comprehensive review of existing literature, providing a basis for new advancements in energy-efficient AI techniques for Fintech applications.

## Chapter 3

# Regulatory Challenges and Compliance in Decentralized Finance (DeFi):

## Comparative Study Between India and USA

V. R. Dhanya

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0009-0003-5541-3486](https://orcid.org/0009-0003-5541-3486)

Christ University, India

Rivika Richard D'silva

Christ University, India

David Joseph

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7493-4362](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7493-4362)

Christ University, India

### ABSTRACT

Decentralized Finance (DeFi) is an emerging force transforming the global financial landscape by leveraging blockchain technology to eradicate the middlemen and assist peer-to-peer financial transactions. However, a decentralized and pseudonymous nature brings a big challenge in its regulation and compliance, especially in Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) regulations, market misconduct and adaptation, new cryptocurrency innovations, and safety and security issues. This paper comparatively analyses the two regulatory frameworks, compliance mechanisms, technical adaptations, and measures of cybersecurity regulating DeFi in India and the United States. By examining the salient regulatory challenges and compliance strategies in both jurisdictions, this study aims to provide insights that help foster a balanced regulatory environment that promotes innovation without undermining financial stability or consumer protection.

### INTRODUCTION

Decentralized Finance, often referred to as DeFi, represents a paradigm shift in the financial sector through the use of blockchain technology, enabling individuals to access financial services without intermediaries like banks or brokers (Werner et al., 2021). DeFi platforms allow activities such as lending, borrowing, trading, and investing, all of which are facilitated by smart contracts deployed on blockchain networks, primarily Ethereum (Harvey et al., 2021). However, the decentralized and pseudonymous nature of DeFi creates significant regulatory and compliance challenges. Enforcing regulations and ensuring compliance within DeFi is difficult due to the absence of centralized control and the anonymity of participants (Zohar, 2021). This paper aims to conduct a comparative analysis of the regulatory challenges and compliance mechanisms of DeFi in India and the USA, examining factors such as technical adaptation, cryptocurrency integration, and cybersecurity, with a particular emphasis on the potential role of machine learning (ML) techniques to address these challenges.

This comparative study's technical and political motivations lie in the distinct trajectories of DeFi adoption and regulation in India and the USA. Technically, India and the USA exhibit significant differences in their levels of blockchain adoption, cryptocurrency integration, and cybersecurity infrastructure. As the hub for fintech innovation, India grapples with limited blockchain adoption due to infrastructure constraints and regulatory ambiguities. On the other hand, in the USA, more advanced technological ecosystems provide a fertile ground for DeFi experimentation and innovation in a fragmented regulatory landscape. Politically, India’s regulatory approach has been conservative in its quest to protect financial stability and consumer protection. In contrast, the USA encourages innovation and protects global financial supremacy with investor protection. These divergent approaches make a comparative analysis essential to understanding how technical and political factors influence regulatory strategies, innovation, and operational outcomes in DeFi.

DeFi represents a new financial ecosystem that operates on decentralized blockchain networks, particularly on Ethereum and other smart contract platforms ([Schär, 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor232)). Unlike the traditional financial system, which relies on centralized intermediaries like banks, exchanges, and brokerages to facilitate transactions, DeFi enables peer-to-peer (P2P) transactions via self-executing smart contracts. These contracts automatically execute transactions when predefined conditions are met, eliminating the need for intermediaries (Harvey et al., 2021).

One of DeFi's most revolutionary aspects is its potential to democratize access to financial services. Individuals with internet access can participate in activities such as lending, borrowing, trading, and earning interest without the need for traditional banking infrastructure ([Schär, 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor232)). This innovation opens doors for unbanked and underbanked populations, providing them with opportunities to access financial services from which they were previously excluded (Werner et al., 2021).

Moreover, DeFi promotes transparency and security. This is also being supported by machine learning algorithms, which further help in identifying anomalies in transaction patterns, predicting potential vulnerabilities, and optimizing smart contract functionality. Transactions and smart contracts are publicly recorded on the blockchain, making them visible to all participants and holding users accountable, which can discourage fraudulent activities (Zohar, 2021). The decentralized nature of these systems also makes them more resilient, as they are less vulnerable to single points of failure, reducing the risk of external attacks or system crashes (Harvey et al., 2021).

This paper aims to explore these dynamics through qualitative methodology, involving in-depth analysis of DeFi regulations in India and the USA through case studies and research papers. The objectives of the research include:

*   • Analyse and compare the regulatory approaches toward Decentralized Finance (DeFi) in India and the USA
    
*   • Explore the challenges of implementing Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) regulations within decentralized systems in both jurisdictions.
    
*   • To Assess Technical Adaptation and Cryptocurrency Integration
    
*   • Examine the risks of market misconduct and fraud within DeFi platforms in both countries, focusing on price manipulation, flash loan attacks, and regulatory gaps.
    
*   • Assess the current state of cybersecurity in DeFi platforms in India and the USA, with a focus on vulnerabilities in smart contracts and other DeFi-related technologies.
    
*   • Investigate how ML techniques can improve compliance, fraud detection, and cybersecurity in DeFi ecosystems.
    

DeFi is revolutionizing the existing financial structure with blockchain technology. Using this technology, DeFi now offers alternative finance options. However, the regulatory landscape remains highly fragmented; India and the USA, for instance, have developed distinct approaches to shaping the sector differently. In India, regulation is vague and restrictive, while in the USA, the regulatory environment is complex, and yet seems more structured and permissive. The cross-border operation of DeFi projects raises major issues, including compliance, barriers to innovation, and concerns about investor protection. Machine learning can address these challenges by offering predictive analytics for regulatory compliance and fraud detection, enabling platforms to adapt to varying legal environments more effectively.

This paper identifies specific regulatory challenges of DeFi in India and the USA, analyzing their impact on efficient operations and market growth, and exploring implications for harmonizing global regulatory systems. Specifically, it examines how these regulatory challenges affect the strategic and operational choices made by DeFi platforms as well as their impact on growth, innovation, and cross-border operations. Finally, the study explores possible paths for harmonizing DeFi regulations between India and the USA that might help with globalization and foster innovation. By integrating machine learning-driven insights, this research aims to propose actionable solutions for compliance and operational efficiency.

By addressing these objectives and motivations, this paper aims to provide policymakers, industry stakeholders, and researchers with actionable insights into the evolving regulatory landscape of DeFi, ultimately contributing to a more harmonized and innovative global financial ecosystem.

### LITERATURE REVIEW

Decentralized Finance (DeFi) represents a transformative shift in the financial landscape, offering an alternative financial architecture where individuals can autonomously lend, borrow, or exchange digital assets using blockchain technology. Unlike Centralized Finance (CeFi), which relies on intermediaries such as banks and financial institutions, DeFi eliminates these intermediaries through smart contracts—self-executing agreements coded on blockchain networks, particularly Ethereum ([Chohan, 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor225); Werner et al., 2021). This shift introduces benefits such as enhanced transparency, accessibility, and reduced transaction costs, yet presents critical challenges in security, regulatory compliance, and scalability ([Rejeb et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor230)).

A key distinction between DeFi and CeFi lies in their operational frameworks. While CeFi depends on centralized entities to mediate financial transactions, DeFi operates through peer-to-peer networks, eliminating the need for centralized control. This structural difference positions DeFi as a more transparent and efficient system, yet one that is inherently more susceptible to systemic risks such as smart contract vulnerabilities and regulatory ambiguity ([Qin et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor229)). Previous studies have highlighted both the strengths and weaknesses of DeFi through SWOT analyses, identifying its inclusivity and transparency as major advantages, while pointing out security vulnerabilities and the absence of a standardized regulatory framework as significant limitations ([Rejeb et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor230)).

The decentralized and pseudonymous nature of DeFi presents substantial regulatory challenges across jurisdictions, as traditional compliance measures like Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) are difficult to enforce (Uzougbo et al., 2024). In the United States, regulatory bodies like the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) are actively engaging with DeFi platforms to integrate them into existing legal frameworks. For example, the SEC’s classification of certain DeFi tokens as securities imposes compliance obligations that conflict with the decentralized ethos of these platforms ([Xiong et al., 2023](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor233)). Despite these issues, the relatively permissive and fragmented regulatory environment in the USA has allowed platforms like Uniswap and Aave to thrive by employing innovative mechanisms such as liquidity pools, and automated market-making. ([Gudgeon et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor228)).

India’s regulatory stance, by contrast, is characterized by caution and restriction. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has consistently expressed concerns over cryptocurrencies, associating them with risks to financial stability and consumer protection ([Aithal & Bhuvana, 2020](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor221)). [Chhabra (2023)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor224) highlights how India’s vague and restrictive regulatory environment has stifled the growth of DeFi projects, creating barriers to innovation and technological adoption. While the USA’s fragmented yet progressive regulatory framework facilitates experimentation, India’s conservative approach hinders the development of a robust DeFi ecosystem.

Smart contracts, which are central to DeFi operations, automate financial transactions and reduce reliance on intermediaries, offering increased efficiency and reduced costs (Kaur et al., 2023). However, vulnerabilities in poorly audited smart contracts can lead to significant financial losses, as demonstrated by several high-profile hacking incidents (Werner et al., 2021). In the USA, the rapid adoption of sophisticated DeFi protocols such as Compound and MakerDAO exemplifies the critical role of smart contracts, while also exposing the platforms to technological risks. India, on the other hand, faces infrastructural and regulatory challenges that hinder the widespread deployment of smart contracts, limiting its ability to capitalize on the technological advancements in DeFi ([Chhabra, 2023](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor224)). Integrating machine learning algorithms for smart contract auditing could mitigate these risks by identifying potential vulnerabilities before exploitation.

Cybersecurity concerns further exacerbate the challenges faced by DeFi in both jurisdictions. High-profile cyberattacks, such as flash loan exploits and rug pulls on U.S.-based platforms, highlight the vulnerabilities inherent in DeFi systems ([Amler et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor222)). As DeFi protocols grow in scale and complexity, their exposure to malicious actors increases, necessitating robust cybersecurity frameworks to ensure long-term sustainability ([Gudgeon et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor228)). In India, the absence of adequate cybersecurity measures leaves the DeFi ecosystem highly vulnerable to attacks, further discouraging domestic adoption and innovation ([Chhabra, 2023](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor224)). The application of machine learning techniques, such as anomaly detection and predictive analytics, could strengthen cybersecurity defences by identifying and mitigating potential threats in real time.

The literature also highlights significant gaps in the harmonization of global regulatory frameworks for DeFi. While Uzougbo et al. (2024) and [Xiong et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor233) provide valuable insights into KYC and AML compliance challenges, they do not fully address the socio-political factors shaping regulatory approaches in different jurisdictions. Similarly, [Chohan (2021)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor225) and Werner et al. (2021) offer a comprehensive analysis of the technological and operational aspects of DeFi but overlook the geopolitical implications of regulatory policies. This research seeks to address these gaps by conducting a comparative analysis of regulatory challenges in India and the USA, examining their impact on market growth, innovation, cross-border operations, and exploring how machine learning can serve as a tool for bridging compliance and operational gaps.

By synthesizing existing literature on the technical, regulatory, and cybersecurity challenges of DeFi, this study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of the contrasting regulatory approaches in these two jurisdictions. The findings are expected to contribute to the broader discourse on harmonizing global regulatory standards, fostering innovation, and addressing the inherent risks associated with decentralized finance.

### METHODOLOGY

This study utilizes a qualitative research methodology to explore the regulatory frameworks governing Decentralized Finance (DeFi) in India and the United States. Secondary data from academic journals, government reports, and policy documents are reviewed to understand the regulatory trends, challenges, and frameworks shaping DeFi in both jurisdictions. The focus is on the regulatory environment, KYC/AML compliance, market misconduct, technical adaptation, and cybersecurity.

A qualitative approach was deliberately chosen over quantitative methods due to the complexity and contextual nature of DeFi regulations. While quantitative analysis is useful for statistical examination, it cannot capture the socio-political, legal, and economic factors affecting regulatory decisions. The qualitative approach allows for a detailed exploration of policy intentions, expert insights, and case studies, providing a deeper understanding of how regulations impact market behavior, innovation, and decentralization.

This study delves into the regulatory challenges and compliance mechanisms of Decentralized Finance (DeFi) in India and the United States, focusing on a detailed comparative analysis of critical aspects influencing the DeFi ecosystem in these jurisdictions. The research addresses the following topics:

*   • Regulatory Environment: Comparative evaluation of the overarching regulatory frameworks, highlighting the USA’s structured yet fragmented approach versus India’s cautious and restrictive stance.
    
*   • KYC/AML Compliance: Analysis of the implementation and enforcement of Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) requirements within decentralized systems in both countries.
    
*   • Market Misconduct and Fraud: Exploration of mechanisms to prevent and address issues such as price manipulation, flash loan attacks, and other fraudulent activities in DeFi markets.
    
*   • Technical Adaptation and Integration with Cryptocurrency: Examination of the technological readiness and integration of DeFi platforms with cryptocurrencies, including infrastructural and operational challenges.
    
*   • Cybersecurity: Assessment of cybersecurity vulnerabilities and strategies employed to mitigate risks associated with smart contracts and platform security.
    
*   • Case Studies: Comparative analysis of prominent DeFi platforms, including Uniswap and Aave from the USA, and CoinSwitch Kuber and WazirX from India, to understand their regulatory compliance, operational strategies, and market impact.
    

The study identifies the synergies and disparities in the regulatory and operational landscapes of India and the USA through these topics and offers insights into their implications for global DeFi adoption, innovation, and regulatory harmonization.

### COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS

#### Regulatory Environment

India’s cautious and ambiguous approach to DeFi stems from the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) concerns about unregulated cryptocurrencies and decentralized financial systems. While the RBI explores Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT), the absence of specific regulatory guidelines creates uncertainty, stifling innovation and cross-border operations. According to Aithal & Bhuvana, 2020, lack of clarity in the area limits scalability, discourages global collaboration, and impedes the integration of new financial technologies.

Conversely, the USA follows a more organized yet segmented regulation approach. The regulatory mechanisms here involve agencies such as the SEC and CFTC that actively regulate the DeFi ecosystem under the law of securities and commodities, respectively. While this ensures some regulatory clarity, Werner et al. (2021) argue that the involvement of multiple agencies and varying state-level regulations creates a compliance maze, mirroring the challenges faced by India’s undefined policies. For example, while India’s vagueness may discourage experimentation, the USA’s regulatory complexity hinders seamless expansion for platforms like Compound. Both countries face scalability challenges but for different reasons: India’s unclear rules and the USA’s overregulation.

#### KYC/AML Compliance

This is an enormous challenge for the adoption of KYC and AML protocols in DeFi both in India and the USA, given the pseudonymous nature of blockchain transactions

In India, KYC/AML policies are strictly implemented in traditional finance but not so in DeFi. [Aithal & Bhuvana (2020)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor221) mention that such a gap makes Indian DeFi platforms vulnerable to fraud and money laundering. Besides, the lack of uniform regulations intensifies compliance difficulties and requires platforms to use patchwork approaches. Machine learning (ML) offers significant potential to address these issues by enabling real-time transaction monitoring, detecting suspicious activity through anomaly detection algorithms, and enhancing pseudonymous identity verification without compromising user privacy.

Similarly, the USA has the same challenges despite having very sophisticated regulatory mechanisms. The Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and guidance from FinCEN enforce strict AML requirements, yet the decentralized nature of DeFi complicates their implementation. [Xiong et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor233) highlight that embedding KYC/AML protocols into smart contracts could resolve this issue. However, as Werner et al. (2021) suggest, while this approach might work in the USA, its adoption in India could be hindered by the lack of infrastructure and technical expertise. Machine learning-based systems in the USA could further streamline KYC/AML compliance by automating document verification and using predictive models to flag potential fraud risks. The USA’s focus on innovation contrasts sharply with India’s struggle for foundational regulatory clarity.

#### Market Misconduct and Fraud

Market misconduct, such as price manipulation and flash loan attacks, is becoming a source of concern in DeFi globally.

The deFi market in India is relatively small, and few cases of fraud or manipulation have been noticed so far. As [Salami (2021)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor231) cautions, however, the risk of price manipulation can increase manifold if proper regulation and monitoring are not in place. For instance, Indian platforms lack in-depth tools to detect and mitigate flash loan exploits. The vulnerability will possibly be exploited as the market matures. Predictive analytics and transaction pattern recognition tools could help Indian platforms proactively identify and mitigate such risks as the market grows.

On the other hand, the USA experiences frequent and high-profile cases of market misconduct, reflecting its larger and more advanced DeFi ecosystem. [Gudgeon et al. (2020)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor228) describe incidents like flash loan attacks, which exploit protocol vulnerabilities, causing significant financial losses. [Xiong et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor233) argue that the USA’s fragmented regulatory structure complicates efforts to implement uniform oversight, making it challenging to prevent misconduct effectively. Machine learning applications, such as fraud detection algorithms and real-time monitoring systems, can assist in identifying anomalies in trading patterns and curbing misconduct more efficiently in the expansive U.S. ecosystem. While India faces risks from underdevelopment, the USA’s challenges stem from managing a highly dynamic and expansive ecosystem.

#### Technical Adaptation and Integration with Cryptocurrency

Indian DeFi platforms face significant technological integration challenges due to the rigid regulations and infrastructure of the country. While Polygon (Matic) has emerged as a key player, addressing scaling and transaction cost issues through Layer 2 solutions, the broader diffusion of DeFi technologies remains slow. [Aithal & Bhuvana (2020)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor221) argue that this delay reflects the lack of government support for decentralized innovations. In contrast, the USA is at the forefront of DeFi technological advancements. Platforms like Uniswap, Aave, and Compound leverage cutting-edge technologies, such as smart contracts, to enhance efficiency, security, and usability. Kaur et al. (2023) highlight that these innovations set new global standards, positioning the USA as a dominant player in the global DeFi market.

The use of machine learning (ML) in the US DeFi platforms has significantly contributed to their success. ML algorithms are employed to predict price movements, improve liquidity management, and optimize transaction flows, all while maintaining robust security protocols. These advancements have not only enhanced the efficiency of decentralized finance but have also allowed US-based systems to respond swiftly to market dynamics, giving them a competitive edge.

Meanwhile, India's DeFi systems remain constrained by regulatory delays and technological infrastructure gaps. While innovations like Polygon offer solutions, they are often hindered by a regulatory environment that fails to support fast-paced technological adoption. This contrast underscores the need for cautionary yet supportive measures that encourage innovation in India’s DeFi ecosystem. To remain competitive on the global stage, India must embrace a regulatory framework that nurtures technological advancement, potentially integrating machine learning to drive efficiency and enhance the functionality of its DeFi platforms.

#### Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity remains a significant challenge for DeFi platforms in India and the USA.

As of now, nascent DeFi markets are vulnerable, especially in India; the infrastructure for regulations and technological setup is underdeveloped. [Aithal & Bhuvana (2020)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor221) caution that Indian platforms may face massive hacking and fraud challenges if prevalence continues unabated, creating the need to prioritize the establishment of strong cybersecurity frameworks and awareness building among stakeholders over immediate needs. Machine learning (ML) could help by detecting fraudulent patterns and providing predictive insights to prevent attacks.

The USA has made tremendous strides in the area of cybersecurity for DeFi. Leading platforms provide regular smart contract audits and sophisticated monitoring systems. According to [Gudgeon et al. (2020)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch003.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor228), however, rapid innovation is continuously exposing new vulnerabilities. As Kaur et al. (2023) argue, the USA comprehensive approach to cybersecurity, aided by ML, sets the example, but sustaining such momentum requires continued investment in advanced security measures. India needs foundational security, whereas the USA looks for developing its defences with new threats.
