## Chapter 14

# Evaluating the Effectiveness of Optimized LSTM and XGBoost Classifiers in High-Frequency Futures Market Prediction

Haojun Chen

[![Orcid Image](image/orcid-logo.png)https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9168-9234](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9168-9234)

Guangzhou Huali College, China

### ABSTRACT

This study compares the performance of two machine learning models - Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and XGBoost - in high-frequency intraday futures market forecasting. Using historical market data from five major Chinese futures markets, the research evaluates specialized classifiers in terms of prediction accuracy and backtesting profits. The results show that LSTM outperforms XGBoost in volatile markets, such as Crude Oil and Silver Futures, with higher prediction accuracy and risk-adjusted returns. XGBoost, however, demonstrates better stability and efficiency in more stable markets like Soybean and Rebar Futures. Backtesting results suggest that both models can generate high-quality trading signals in real-time, high-frequency trading environments. This study offers insights into applying these classifiers for short-term futures market predictions and provides important implications for high-frequency trading strategies in the Chinese futures market.

### 1\. INTRODUCTION

In the realm of financial market prediction, XGBoost and LSTM are two of the most widely used machine learning models due to their ability to capture complex patterns and dependencies in financial data (e.g. [Chen & Guestrin, 2016](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor866); [Oukhouya, et al., 2024](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor887); [Vuong, et al., 2022](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor894), [Raudys & Goldstein, 2022](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor889)). XGBoost, known for its efficiency in handling structured data and identifying feature interactions, has been successfully applied to tasks such as stock price prediction and asset price forecasting. Similarly, LSTM, with its ability to model temporal dependencies, is frequently employed in time series forecasting, especially for financial market data ([Fischer & Krauss, 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor871)). However, while these models have been extensively used for price forecasting, few studies have employed them specifically as classifiers for predicting very short-term market price direction, such as in high-frequency trading environments. This gap in the literature highlights the potential value of evaluating these models for improving the accuracy and efficiency of real-time market predictions in increasingly automated trading systems.

Predicting the market direction—whether the price will move up or down—offers several practical benefits over predicting absolute price levels, particularly in fast-paced and volatile markets. By focusing on direction, the classification task becomes more robust to market noise and volatility, offering a more reliable basis for real-time trading decisions ([Rouf et al, 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor890)). This approach aligns well with the needs of HFT systems, where buy/sell signals need to be generated instantly in response to rapid market changes. Moreover, market direction prediction allows for the design of more flexible and scalable trading strategies that can react to short-term price movements, rather than relying on the challenging task of forecasting exact price levels ([O’hara, 2015](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor886)). In such systems, accurate classification of market movements forms the foundation for profitable decision-making in an increasingly automated environment.

In this study, we demonstrate the effectiveness of XGBoost and LSTM classifiers for predicting futures market direction using high-frequency market data from the Chinese futures market, which is notable for its rapid growth, increasing liquidity, and emerging role in global commodity trading ([Li et al., 2024](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor884)). The study employs a range of features derived from both real-time market data (such as open interest, price volatility, and bid-ask spreads) and technical indicators (including the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD), Relative Strength Index (RSI), and Stochastic Oscillator), with the goal of improving the accuracy of market direction predictions. A key challenge in financial time series prediction is ensuring that the model generalizes well to future, unseen data, given the temporal nature of the data. To address this, the study employs the Rolling Time-Series Split Validation (RTSV) method, a robust technique for evaluating predictive models on sequential data. Unlike traditional cross-validation methods that shuffle data randomly, the RTSV method respects the temporal order of data, ensuring that models are trained on past data and tested on future data, simulating real-world conditions where past market behavior is used to predict future movements. This approach ensures that the models are optimized for high-frequency prediction tasks, where both temporal dependencies and high volatility are key factors to consider.

The results of this study indicate that LSTM consistently outperforms XGBoost in terms of prediction accuracy and profitability, especially in the context of high-frequency predictions. LSTM demonstrated higher accuracy across all forecast horizons (1-minute, 5-minute, and 15-minute) and outperformed XGBoost in markets with higher volatility, such as Crude Oil Futures and Silver Futures. This performance is attributed to LSTM’s ability to model temporal dependencies, capturing sequential patterns in market data that XGBoost fails to address. LSTM’s superior generalization across different market conditions, especially in volatile environments, suggests that sequential models are better suited for time-sensitive predictions in financial markets.

The performance of both models is also evaluated through backtesting, where out-of-sample actual market data are used to compute trading returns and risk based on real-time prediction signals generated by the two models. LSTM consistently outperforms XGBoost in terms of Adjusted Total Return (which includes trading costs) across all markets and time horizons, demonstrating its superior ability to manage risk and volatility in high-frequency trading environments. While XGBoost is competitive in certain markets, such as Soybean Futures, it generally fails to generate as strong risk-adjusted returns, particularly in more volatile markets like Crude Oil and Silver Futures. These results suggest that LSTM’s ability to capture long-term dependencies and model sequential data makes it better suited for high-frequency market direction prediction tasks, where volatility and market dynamics play a critical role.

However, while LSTM excels in volatility and managing sequential dependencies, it is not without limitations. The model is prone to overfitting, particularly in markets with frequent price fluctuations, such as Crude Oil Futures. Despite this, LSTM maintained better performance on out-of-sample data, demonstrating its robustness in real-world trading scenarios. XGBoost, on the other hand, despite its capability to model feature interactions, struggled with generalizing in high-frequency environments where temporal features play a critical role. This suggests that models like LSTM, which can account for the time-dependent nature of financial markets, have a distinct advantage in tasks involving short-term forecasting.

One of the key implications of this study is the potential for LSTM and XGBoost to complement each other in future research and practical applications. While LSTM is more adept at capturing the sequential patterns of high-frequency data, XGBoost can enhance feature engineering by identifying important market signals that LSTM might overlook. Combining the strengths of both models could lead to more accurate and robust predictions of market direction, particularly in volatile and complex market environments.

This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a comprehensive review of the relevant literature, focusing on previous studies related to high-frequency intraday futures market forecasting and machine learning applications. Section 3 outlines the institutional context, describing the key Chinese futures markets and their characteristics. Section 4 details the data used in this study, including the features derived from both real-time market data and technical indicators. Section 5 presents the methodology, explaining the development, optimization, and evaluation of the LSTM and XGBoost classifiers. Section 6 provides descriptive statistics, highlighting the key characteristics of the data and features used in the study. Section 7 presents the results, offering a comparative analysis of the models in terms of prediction accuracy, profitability, and backtesting performance. Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper by discussing the implications of the findings for high-frequency trading strategies and suggesting areas for future research.

### 2\. LITERATURE REVIEW

The current study aims to contribute to the existing literature on financial market prediction using machine learning (ML) approaches by focusing on comparing the performance of two of the most commonly used ML models - LSTM and XGBoost - in the context of very short-term intraday predictions in futures markets. This comparative study adds to the growing body of work exploring the application of machine learning techniques in forecasting market movements.

LSTM networks, known for their ability to model long-term dependencies and capture sequential patterns, have gained prominence in financial market predictions, particularly for time-series forecasting ([Fischer & Krauss, 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor871)). For example, [Bao et al. (2017)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor865) demonstrated that LSTM models are highly effective in predicting stock market trends, especially in intraday settings, where capturing the dynamics of short-term price changes is crucial. [Guo et al. (2021)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor875) further reinforced this view by applying LSTM networks in more complex financial environments, showing the model’s robustness in handling volatile data typical of intraday futures markets.

In contrast, XGBoost, a widely used gradient boosting algorithm, excels in handling structured data and identifying non-linear relationships between features ([Chen & Guestrin, 2016](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor866)). [Patel et al. (2015)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor888) demonstrated that XGBoost outperforms other models in stock market trend predictions, utilizing structured market data and capturing complex interactions between multiple market features. [Hossain & Kaur (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor878) compared the performance of XGBoost and LSTM for stock price prediction, showing that while XGBoost exhibited superior performance in stability and efficiency, LSTM outperformed in scenarios with complex sequential data. Similarly, [Tian (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor892) examined XGBoost and LSTM for cryptocurrency market prediction, finding that XGBoost outperformed LSTM in terms of mean squared error (MSE) and stable performance, while LSTM was found to be unstable with extreme outliers.

The growing interest in machine learning models for market prediction has led to the increasing trend of integrating technical indicators with these models to enhance predictive accuracy. Technical indicators, such as Moving Averages, RSI, MACD, and Bollinger Bands, have long been utilized in financial markets to capture trends, momentum, and volatility based on historical data ([Achelis, 2001](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor863)). While some scholars have questioned their theoretical foundations, technical indicators remain invaluable tools in algorithmic and high-frequency trading. More recent studies have demonstrated the potential of combining machine learning techniques with technical indicators to improve short-term market predictions. For example, [Fischer and Krauss (2018)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor871) highlighted the effectiveness of LSTM networks in modeling complex, non-linear relationships between price patterns and technical indicators. Other studies, including those by [Jose & Varshini (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor879), [Sharma & Verma (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor891), and [Lee (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor882), have shown that integrating technical indicators with machine learning models can enhance prediction accuracy by capturing the interactions between various market signals, such as momentum and volatility. Additionally, recent research by [Gezici & Sefer (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor873), [Zhang et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor897), and [Wang et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor895) has demonstrated the promising application of deep transformer-based networks for predicting stock movements.

Despite the clear advantages of combining LSTM and XGBoost with technical indicators, most of the literature has focused on long-term predictions or price forecasting, leaving a gap in research focused on short-term directional predictions in high-frequency futures markets. The current study fills this gap by providing a comparative analysis of LSTM and XGBoost classifiers for very short-term directional prediction (1 to 15-minute horizon) in the futures market. This approach extends previous research by incorporating both machine learning classifiers and technical indicators in a high-frequency context. The novelty of this study lies in its focus on high-frequency directional prediction, which remains underexplored in the literature, particularly for the futures market.

This study also contributes to the connection of machine learning literature in the Chinese futures market. The Chinese futures market is notable for its high volatility, significant government influence, and growing liquidity, making it an ideal environment for testing machine learning models ([Li et al., 2024](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor884)). Studies like [He et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor877) have shown that the Chinese commodity futures market is not weak-form efficient, allowing machine learning-based technical analysis to generate excess returns and support high-frequency predictions. [Wang et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor896) introduced a deep learning model for event-driven volatility prediction in the crude oil futures market. [Ke et al. (2023)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor880) proposed an EEMD-Hurst-LSTM hybrid model, which improves predictive performance and informs better trading strategies with high-frequency data. Guo et al. (2022) used machine learning techniques like SVM and XGBoost to predict risk states in China’s crude oil futures market, demonstrating the improved predictive power of their models.

However, despite growing interest in machine learning for the futures market, few studies have focused on directional predictions using classifiers in high frequency trrading. The only study of this kind is [Deng et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor867), who transformed 1-hour frequency futures market predictions into a multi-class classification problem using XGBoost, SMOTE, and NSGA-II techniques. This study, therefore, provides a novel contribution by exploring this underexplored area and providing new insights into short-term directional prediction using machine learning classifiers.

### 3\. INSTITUTIONAL BACKGROUND

The raw dataset for this study consists of high-frequency trading data from five of the most actively traded futures contracts in the Chinese market: Crude Oil Futures, Gold Futures, Soybean Futures, Silver Futures, and Rebar Futures. These contracts are traded on various futures exchanges within China, each with unique characteristics and liquidity profiles that are crucial for understanding market dynamics at high-frequency levels.

The trading hours for the five futures markets vary depending on the exchange and commodity. Crude Oil Futures, Gold Futures, Silver Futures are open from 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM, with a break from 11:30 AM to 1:30 PM, and night trading from 9:00 PM to 2:30 AM. Soybean Futures and Rebar Futures have the similar day trading hours but shorten night trading hours: from 9:00 to 11:00 PM.

Crude Oil Futures are traded on the Shanghai International Energy Exchange (INE), part of the Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE). These contracts play a significant role in the global energy markets, offering investors exposure to fluctuations in crude oil prices. The average annual trading volume of Crude Oil Futures on the INE exceeds 200 million contracts, with each contract representing 1,000 barrels of crude oil.

Gold Futures are also traded on the SHFE and serve as a key instrument for speculating on or hedging against gold price movements. As one of the most popular commodities in the Chinese market, Gold Futures see annual trading volumes surpassing 500 million contracts. Each contract represents 1 kilogram of gold, providing both retail and institutional investors with exposure to gold price dynamics.

Soybean Futures, listed on the Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE), are a major agricultural commodity in China, with high relevance to domestic demand for animal feed and food products. The average annual trading volume of Soybean Futures on the DCE is approximately 150 million contracts. Each contract represents 10 metric tons of soybeans, attracting agricultural investors seeking to hedge or speculate on price changes in this sector.

Silver Futures, another significant commodity traded on the SHFE, focus on speculating and hedging against fluctuations in the silver market. The annual trading volume for Silver Futures often exceeds 100 million contracts, with each contract representing 15 kilograms of silver, offering market participants a means to manage silver price risk.

Rebar Futures, traded on the DCE, are used by investors and industry participants to manage risks related to the price of rebar, a key construction material. Given that China is the world’s largest consumer of steel, Rebar Futures have an average annual trading volume of around 400 million contracts. Each contract represents 10 metric tons of rebar, making it a crucial tool for the construction and manufacturing sectors.

These futures contracts represent some of the most significant commodities in the Chinese market, each with unique characteristics, trading volumes, and contract sizes. The high-frequency trading data derived from these contracts provides valuable insights into market movements and can be leveraged for the development of predictive models and trading strategies. [Deng et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor867) demonstrated the potential of using machine learning classifiers for intraday predictions (at 1-hour frequency) specifically for the Rebar Futures market, highlighting the promising application of machine learning for short-term

### 4\. DATA AND FEATURES

#### 4.1 The Original Data

High-frequency historical market data, with a cross-sectional view of the market, recorded approximately every half second from January 11th, 2024, to September 5th, 2024, were obtained from the futures exchanges' data API. The dataset includes a total of 55,621,318 observations from five futures markets. For each market, the original data were resampled into 1-minute, 5-minute, and 15-minute intervals using a forward-fill approach.

#### 4.2 Features

This study utilizes a variety of features categorized into two primary groups: real-time market data features and technical indicator-based features. These are summarized in two tables. [Table 1](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor857) presents features derived from real-time market data provided by the futures exchanges, including key metrics such as bid-ask spreads, bid and ask volumes, trading volume, and other order book dynamics. On the other hand, [Table 2](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor858) focuses on features based on technical indicators.

Technical indicators are mathematical calculations derived from market data (e.g., price, volume, or open interest) and are widely used in technical analysis to identify trends, momentum, and potential reversals in financial markets. Common examples include the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD), Relative Strength Index (RSI), and Bollinger Bands. While these indicators often lack rigorous theoretical support, they provide actionable insights into market behavior, making them pragmatic tools for traders.

Despite some skepticism within the academic community, technical indicators remain valuable inputs for machine learning (ML) models. ML models are designed to flexibly evaluate the predictive value of features, including those based on heuristics, and assign importance based on empirical performance. Indicators like MACD and RSI can capture complex, non-linear patterns in market data that are difficult to express through traditional methods. Additionally, the integration of technical indicators with theoretically grounded measures can enhance the robustness of ML models. The data-driven nature of ML allows the incorporation of diverse feature types without strict assumptions, improving predictive accuracy.

#### Table 1. Summary of real-time market price and volume data features

 
| Market Data || Features Variables || Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open Interest || openInt\_last || Level of open interest observed at most recent tick |
| --- | --- | --- |
| oi\_change || Change in open interest during the observation window. Open interest reflects the number of outstanding contracts and is a critical measure of market participation and sentiment. |
| OHLC || high\_pct || Percentage differences between the current price and the daily high, low, open prices, respectively. These features help capture relative price movements and market positioning ([Achelis, 2001](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor863)) |
| low\_pct |
| open\_pct |
| lastset\_pct |
| Volume || dvol || A measure of the volume of contracts traded during the observation window. Prior studies suggest that analyzing the relationship between price movements and trading volume can help determine whether a trend is supported by strong market participation (Tan & Ting 2015; [Unger, 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor893); [Li et al. 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor883)). |
| Price Volatility || vola || A measure of price volatility, calculated as the rolling average of squared percentage price changes over a 60-observation window. Volatility is a fundamental indicator of market risk and uncertainty ([Engle, 1982](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor870)). |
| Price Change || pct\_chg || Percentage change in price over the observation interval. This metric directly captures price momentum, a widely used concept in technical analysis and trading strategies ([Dunham, 2012](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor868)). |
| Liquidity || baspread || The bid-ask spread refers to the difference between the highest price buyers are willing to pay (bid) and the lowest price sellers are willing to accept (ask), where a narrower spread typically indicates higher liquidity and a wider spread signals low liquidity or uncertainty ([Hasbrouck, 1991](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor876)). |
| baVol || Bid and ask volumes reflect the quantities available at these prices, providing insights into market sentiment and order flow imbalances. These features can be used to predict short-term futures market returns as they capture liquidity and sentiment dynamics ([Easley & O’Hara, 1987](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor869)). |

#### Table 2. Summary of features based on technical indicators

| Technical Indicators || Related Features || Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MACD (fast=12, slow=26, signal=9) || MACD line, MACD signal line, and MACD histogram || The MACD system include two components— MACD line, MACD signal line, and MACD histogram. The relative positions between MACD Line and Signal Line are indicative of potential trading signals and the MACD histogram representatives the momentum's rate of change: A growing histogram indicates strengthening momentum, while a shrinking histogram suggests weakening momentum. The values of these MACD components are included in the feature collection. |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RSI (length=14) || RSI || RSI is a popular momentum oscillator used in technical analysis to measure the speed and magnitude of recent price changes. It ranges from 0 to 100 and is primarily used to identify overbought or oversold conditions, as well as potential reversals in price trends. |
| Stochastic Oscillator (length=14) || StoFASTK, StoFASTD || The Stochastic Oscillator is a momentum indicator used in technical analysis to compare a security's closing price to its price range over a specified period. It helps identify overbought or oversold conditions and potential trend reversals. StoFASTK and StoFASTKed are variations of the Stochastic Oscillator. The relative positions of the technical indicators are considered indictors of buy/sell signals and market oversold/overbought conditions. |
| ADX || ADX || ADX (Average Directional Index) is a popular technical indicator used to measure the strength of a trend, regardless of its direction. The ADX ranges from 0 to 100, with higher values indicating a stronger trend. It is calculated based on two other components: the Positive Directional Index (+DI) and the Negative Directional Index (-DI). |
| MFI (length=14) || MFI || MFI (Money Flow Index) is a momentum indicator that incorporates price and volume data to measure buying and selling pressure. It is often called the “volume-weighted RSI” because it is similar to the Relative Strength Index (RSI) but includes volume in its calculation. |
| Moving Averages || DMA30, DMA60, DMA120, DMA240 || These feature values calculated as the distances between the current price and moving averages over four selected windows- 30, 60, 120, and 240 periods. Distance to moving averages has been considered a crucial measure for identifying price deviations from trends and potential reversion opportunities ([Achelis, 2001](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor863); [Gu et al., 2020](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor874)). |

In addition to the features presented in [Table 1](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor857) and [Table 2](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor858), the following features have been engineered from the original data:

*   • Lagged Features
    

Lagged values of price, open interest, volume changes, and volatility are generated for up to 20 lags to incorporate historical context into the dataset. These lagged variables, which include percentage price changes, trading volume, and volatility, are essential for capturing temporal dependencies and momentum effects, as emphasized by Lo and MacKinlay (1998). By using these lagged features, the model can better account for past market conditions and improve its prediction capabilities.

*   • Cyclical Encoding of Intervals
    

The intervals variable, representing 15-minute segments of the trading session, is encoded using cyclical transformations. Each interval is mapped to sine and cosine components (interval\_sin, interval\_cos) as follows:

Interval\_sin = $sin\\left( \\frac{2\\pi\*interval\\\_ index}{N} \\right)$, Interval\_cos = $cos\\left( \\frac{2\\pi\*interval\\\_ index}{N} \\right)$

where N is the total number of unique intervals, including the two opening market auctions. This transformation allows the model to recognize that intervals near the start of the session (e.g., 8:45 PM) are close to the last interval of the previous session. Intraday time effects are significant in the Chinese futures market, where specific intervals, such as the opening auctions at 8:45 PM and 8:45 AM, exhibit unique price behavior due to concentrated market activity (Cao, Hansch, and Wang, 2009).

#### 4.3 Target Variables

The study focuses on the classification ML models for predicting future direction of price movements. The target variables are the future one step ahead direction of the market price move, with 1 indicating the positive direction and 0 for the negative direction. To avoid classic imbalance, observations with 0 price changes in the target variables are removed from model training.

#### 4.4 Standardization

All numerical features, except for the cyclically encoded features interval\_sin and interval\_cos, are standardized using the formular below:

$z = \\frac{x - u}{\\sigma}$

Where z is the standardized value of the feature, x is the original value, u is the mean, estimated by the training sample average, and *σ* is the standard deviation, estimated by the training sample standard deviation. Standardization ensures that these features have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. This step is crucial to bring all features to a comparable scale, particularly when they have different units and ranges, as is common in financial data.

### 5\. METHODOLOGY

The dynamic and high-frequency nature of the futures market demands predictive models capable of capturing both complex feature interactions and sequential temporal patterns. This study employs XGBoost and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, as these algorithms complement each other in addressing these challenges. XGBoost excels at identifying non-linear relationships within structured datasets featuring engineered predictors, while LSTM is designed to effectively model temporal dependencies and sequential patterns inherent in trading data. This section provides an overview of Classification algorithms under the context of the current study, where accuracy is the key performance measure due to the nature of market predictions.

#### 5.1 XGBoost Classifier

The XGBoost classifier improves prediction accuracy through an iterative process known as gradient boosting, where multiple decision trees are trained sequentially ([Chen & Guestrin, 2016](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor866)). Initially, the first tree produces raw scores, which represent the model's confidence in predicting the likelihood of each class (for example, whether the market will rise or fall). These raw scores, which are essentially log-odds, are transformed into probabilities using the sigmoid function. With each new tree added to the model, it focuses on correcting the residuals, or errors, made by the previous trees. In this way, the model iteratively adjusts and improves its predictions, refining its accuracy at each step. The raw scores from each tree are combined, and the sum is passed through the sigmoid function to produce the final predicted probabilities. This process continues until the model achieves optimal performance in terms of prediction accuracy, balancing the trade-off between bias and variance.

Accuracy is the key performance measure for XGBoost in this study, as the model’s goal is to predict the correct market direction with high precision. To optimize this accuracy, XGBoost minimizes log-loss, also known as binary cross-entropy, which measures the discrepancy between the predicted probabilities and the true class labels. Log-loss penalizes the model more heavily for confident but incorrect predictions, encouraging the model to produce well-calibrated probabilities. By iteratively correcting errors and optimizing for accuracy, XGBoost ensures that the final model performs robustly, with improved prediction performance at each iteration.

#### 5.2 LSTM Network Classifier

In this study, a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is employed as a classifier for binary classification tasks. LSTM networks are particularly well-suited for sequential data, as they are capable of capturing long-term dependencies, which is critical in predicting market direction based on time series data. The model architecture for classification consists of three main components:

*   • LSTM Layer: The LSTM layer processes the sequential input data, retaining information over time through memory cells. These memory cells help capture long-term patterns, which are crucial for accurate classification in time series problems like predicting market movement.
    
*   • Dropout Layer: A dropout layer is included for regularization, randomly deactivating neurons during training to prevent overfitting and improve the model’s ability to generalize to unseen data (Srivastava et al., 2014).
    
*   • Dense Layer with Sigmoid Activation: The output layer is a dense layer with a sigmoid activation function, which maps the model’s raw output to a probability value between 0 and 1, representing the likelihood that the sample belongs to a particular class.
    

The LSTM model is optimized using the Adam optimizer, which adjusts the learning rates of each parameter dynamically during training ([Kingma & Ba, 2015](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor881)). This helps the model converge efficiently, even when gradients are sparse or noisy. The model uses binary cross\-entropy as the loss function, which measures the difference between the predicted probabilities and the true class labels. This loss function guides the model to minimize prediction errors, improving the accuracy of its binary classification. The model's performance is evaluated using the accuracy score, which tracks the proportion of correct predictions made during training and testing. Accuracy is critical in this context, as it reflects how well the model can predict the market direction, ensuring that the model's predictions align with the true outcomes. By iterating through these steps—updating gradients through Adam, minimizing loss through binary cross-entropy, and tracking performance via accuracy—the model learns to classify data more effectively with each epoch, ultimately optimizing the classifier's performance for high-frequency market predictions.

#### 5.3 Cross-Validation and Hyperparameter Turning

This study begins by dividing the full dataset into training and test periods using an 80:20 split, based on daily intervals. The best model, with the highest accuracy score, is selected from the training period through a Rolling Time-Series Split Validation (RTSV) method for hyperparameter tuning and is subsequently evaluated on the test set. [Table 3](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor859) summarizes the hyperparameter tuning configuration in this study.

#### Table 3. Summary of hyperparameter tuning configuration

 
| Hyperparameter || Tuning Range || Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| XGBoost |
| --- |
| learning\_rate || \[0.001, 0.3\] || step size at each iteration while moving toward a minimum of the loss function, with smaller values leading to more gradual updates and potentially better generalization, but requiring more boosting rounds to converge. |
| max\_depth || \[3, 9\] || specifies the maximum depth of each decision tree, controlling the complexity of the model; deeper trees can capture more intricate patterns but may lead to overfitting, while shallower trees might underfit the data. |
| LSTM |
| units || \[20, 300\] || determines the capacity of the model to capture and store information. A higher number of units allows the network to learn more complex patterns and relationships from the data, but can also increase the risk of overfitting and computational cost. |
| dropout\_rate || \[0.1, 0.9\] || a regularization technique used to prevent overfitting by randomly setting a fraction of input units to zero during training |
| epochs || \[5, 100\] || defines the number of complete passes through the training dataset during model training. |
| batch\_size || \[32, 64\] || determines the number of training samples used in one forward/backward pass of the model. |

Within the training period, the initial training window is set to include 80% of the data from the earlier part of the timeline. Candidate classifiers are trained using this training set, and their performance is assessed based on observations from the trade day immediately following the training window. The training window and the corresponding test trade day are then moved forward incrementally, continuing this process until the end of the data period is reached.

#### 5.4 The Optimized Classifiers

The RTSV method is tailored for sequential data, such as time series. Unlike traditional cross-validation methods, which randomly shuffle and partition data, rolling validation respects the temporal order of observations, making it particularly suitable for financial datasets where intertemporal relationships are crucial. Studies such as Bergmeir et al. (2018) highlight the importance of preserving temporal order in cross-validation for time-series data, noting that random shuffling can lead to misleadingly optimistic performance estimates.

However, the RTSV method is not without limitations. A significant drawback is its computational intensity¹. Each fold requires retraining the model on an increasingly larger training set, which can be resource-intensive for complex algorithms such as XGBoost and LSTM. For example, models like LSTM involve iterative backpropagation over time, and retraining multiple times can substantially increase the computational load. Furthermore, the overlap in training data across folds can lead to redundancy, as the model may repeatedly encounter similar patterns, potentially limiting the diversity of insights gained from the validation process. Another limitation is the reduced size of the validation set in earlier folds, which may not represent the full range of temporal patterns, leading to biased performance evaluations.

Despite these challenges, rolling validation provides a realistic assessment of the model's predictive performance by simulating the process of using historical data to forecast future events. In the context of this study, rolling validation ensures that the hyperparameters for XGBoost and LSTM are optimized in a manner consistent with the temporal nature of the futures market data. This approach balances the need for robust evaluation with the computational demands inherent in high-frequency financial modeling. By adhering to the principles of rolling validation, this study aligns its methodology with best practices in time-series analysis, as emphasized in works such as Hyndman and Athanasopoulos (2021) and Bergmeir et al. (2018).

### 6\. DESCRIPTIVE STATISTICS

Tables of descriptive statistics for key real-time market data features for five futures markets - crude oil, gold, soybean, silver, and rebar - are presented in the appendices. The dataset provides a comprehensive perspective, highlighting the unique market characteristics of each futures contract. These differences reflect the distinct economic roles, trading dynamics, and investor behaviors associated with each commodity.

Crude Oil Futures exhibit significant variability in key market indicators, especially in terms of volume and open interest. Notably, the volume shows extreme fluctuations, reflecting the high liquidity of the market, while open interest is consistently high, indicating robust market participation. The volatility of the Crude Oil Futures market is evident, with considerable variation in volatility across the different time frequencies. At 1-minute intervals, the volatility is relatively low but steadily increases at longer time frames, indicating greater market movement and risk over time. The basis spread, which indicates the price difference between contracts, maintains a narrow range but has occasional spikes, illustrating periods of heightened market uncertainty or liquidity changes.

Gold Futures, while similarly volatile, display more stability in terms of open interest compared to Crude Oil. The market for Gold Futures is characterized by its slightly lower price range and relatively more consistent volume, with large fluctuations being less common. The basis spread is generally narrow but shows occasional widening, likely reflecting changes in market sentiment or other external factors. Volatility in Gold Futures remains relatively subdued across all time intervals, indicating a more stable market environment. Unlike Crude Oil, Gold Futures tend to have smaller average percentage changes, signaling less erratic price movements on average, with occasional sharp deviations when significant news events impact investor sentiment.

Soybean Futures stand out for their high-volume variability, with extreme volume values that highlight the market’s sensitivity to demand and supply shocks, which is common in agricultural commodities. Soybean Futures also demonstrate high levels of open interest, signaling a well-established market with significant investor activity. The basis spread is strikingly wide, remaining at a consistent value of 1.00 across frequencies, but with notable spikes that suggest changes in supply and demand dynamics. Volatility is moderate compared to other markets, with small fluctuations in price at 1-minute intervals, but it becomes more pronounced over longer periods, indicating more substantial price shifts. The market's relatively larger average price and broader price range compared to other commodities reflect the distinct dynamics of agricultural commodities, where weather and seasonality can have a profound impact.

Silver Futures reveal a higher degree of volatility, especially at the 1-minute frequency, which shows noticeable spikes in both price and volume. The average price of Silver Futures is significantly higher than that of Gold and Soybean Futures, indicating its position as a more premium commodity within the metals market. The open interest in Silver is comparable to that of Soybean Futures, with high levels suggesting a deep and active market. The basis spread is slightly wider than that of Gold, reflecting greater fluctuations in contract prices. Volatility in the Silver Futures market is more pronounced compared to both Gold and Soybean, with values that increase substantially across longer time intervals, underscoring the inherent risk and market dynamics that are often linked to investor behavior and geopolitical factors. Additionally, Silver Futures display the largest percentage changes, demonstrating more dramatic price swings, a characteristic feature of precious metals markets that are sensitive to macroeconomic trends.

Rebar Futures, primarily driven by the construction industry, show a distinctive profile with relatively lower volatility compared to other markets. The average prices in Rebar Futures are in the mid-range compared to the other commodities, with less extreme fluctuations. While volume is substantial, it does not reach the same peaks seen in the Crude Oil or Soybean markets, but it still reflects significant trading activity. The open interest in Rebar Futures is also relatively high, suggesting a stable and mature market, with the basis spread typically staying close to 1.00, showing a lack of sharp price changes or sudden market shifts. The volatility, though lower than that of Silver and Crude Oil, shows moderate changes across the different time frequencies, which is typical for a market tied to the industrial sector. The percentage change in Rebar Futures is generally smaller than in other markets, indicating a market with less dramatic price movements on average.

Overall, while all five markets demonstrate periods of high volatility and fluctuations, each has its unique characteristics. Crude Oil and Silver Futures are more sensitive to global economic and geopolitical events, often showing higher volatility and larger price movements. Gold and Soybean Futures, on the other hand, tend to experience more stability, with Gold reflecting the traditional “safe haven” role in times of uncertainty. Soybean, being an agricultural commodity, is more influenced by seasonal and climatic factors. Rebar Futures, tied to the construction sector, exhibit less volatility and smaller price changes, indicative of the more stable nature of industrial commodity markets.

### 7\. RESULTS AND PERFORMANCE COMPARISON

#### 7.1 Prediction Accuracy

The results reveal that LSTM consistently outperforms XGBoost across all markets and forecast horizons, particularly for the shorter timeframes. For example, in the 1-minute ahead prediction, LSTM achieved test accuracies ranging from 0.65 in Silver Futures to 0.74 in Rebar Futures, while XGBoost showed test accuracies ranging from 0.52 (in Silver Futures) to 0.66 (in Soybean Futures). This trend holds across the other horizons, with LSTM maintaining higher accuracy overall, especially in more volatile markets like Crude Oil Futures and Silver Futures, where XGBoost struggled to achieve strong performance. The gap in performance between the two models is most pronounced in the 15-minute ahead predictions, where LSTM demonstrates better generalization across all markets, while XGBoost’s performance deteriorates, especially in markets with higher volatility.

Several factors can explain these differences in performance. One of LSTM's key strengths is its ability to handle sequential data and capture long-term dependencies. Unlike XGBoost, which treats each observation independently and lacks an inherent mechanism for modeling time-based relationships, LSTM is specifically designed to model the temporal dynamics inherent in time-series data, such as those found in high-frequency financial markets. The ability of LSTM to capture sequential dependencies enables it to better track market movements and volatility patterns over time, which is essential for accurate prediction in short-term forecasting. Additionally, the features used by both models, including Open Interest, Volume, Price Volatility, and Liquidity, reflect underlying market sentiment and price movements that are inherently time dependent. LSTM’s capacity to capture the interactions between these time-dependent features—such as cyclical encoding for time intervals—helps model market behaviors tied to specific times of day, like the opening and closing prices. In contrast, while XGBoost processes the same features, it lacks a natural mechanism for modeling these time-based dependencies, which limits its effectiveness as the forecast horizon extends.

Another reason for LSTM’s superior performance lies in its ability to handle volatility and liquidity shifts, common in high-frequency financial data. Features such as the bid-ask spread and market depth reflect short-term market conditions, and LSTM is better able to learn how sudden changes in liquidity or volatility signal upcoming price movements. This capacity is particularly important in markets like Crude Oil Futures, where price fluctuations can be influenced by microstructural changes, such as shifts in liquidity. In contrast, XGBoost, being a tree-based model, may not be as sensitive to these rapid market shifts, and as a result, it struggles to capture the underlying dynamics effectively, especially when these dynamics change quickly.

The observed differences in training accuracy suggest that LSTM may be overfitting to the training data, particularly in volatile markets like Crude Oil Futures, where rapid price and liquidity fluctuations are frequent. However, despite this overfitting, LSTM still generalizes well to unseen data, as evidenced by its consistently higher test accuracy. This suggests that LSTM is adept at leveraging temporal relationships and patterns, which helps it generalize better to new data. On the other hand, XGBoost, while capable of modeling complex feature interactions, seems to struggle with generalization when dealing with high-frequency data, where temporal dependencies and the influence of time-based features are more significant.

In conclusion, the results indicate that LSTM is better suited for high-frequency prediction tasks in futures markets, especially when predicting short-term price movements. Its ability to model sequential data, capture long-term dependencies, and incorporate time-based features like cyclical encoding provides it with a clear advantage over XGBoost, which struggles to handle these aspects. The performance gap is most noticeable in volatile markets and longer prediction horizons, where LSTM can capture subtle shifts in market dynamics that XGBoost fails to model effectively. Future research could explore hybrid models that combine the strengths of both approaches, integrating LSTM’s sequential learning with XGBoost’s robust feature engineering capabilities, to improve prediction accuracy in high-frequency financial markets.

#### 7.2 Black-Testing Performance

When evaluating machine learning models, accuracy scores (or confusion matrices) alone often do not provide a complete picture of their effectiveness, especially in financial market prediction tasks. While accuracy can indicate how often a model’s predictions align with actual market movements, it fails to capture the financial viability of those predictions. In practical trading, the true measure of a model’s performance is not just its accuracy, but its ability to generate profitable outcomes, considering both the magnitude of returns and the associated risk. This is where back testing performance becomes crucial. By simulating how each model’s predictions would have translated into actual trades over time, back testing provides a more comprehensive evaluation of a model's true effectiveness, considering real-world trading conditions.

[Table 5](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor861) compares the performance of the LSTM and XGBoost models in terms of profitability, based on backtesting results that follow the direction signals provided by the optimized classification model. The key performance metrics include Mean Return, Return Standard Deviation (Return Std.), Total Return, and Adjusted Total Return. Returns are calculated as percentages based on the last closing prices, following the market direction predictions from the optimized trained model. The Adjusted Total Return accounts for market-specific trading costs, offering a more realistic measure of profitability by incorporating transaction fees, slippage, and other market frictions. It is crucial to emphasize the relationship between Return and Risk, as reflected in the Return Std., which quantifies the risk level associated with each model's predictions. A model that generates higher returns but also exhibits higher volatility may signal greater risk exposure, whereas a model with more stable returns and lower volatility may offer safer, albeit smaller, profits. Understanding this trade-off is essential when evaluating the models' effectiveness in practical, high-risk environments like financial markets.

(0.164) compared to LSTM's (0.15) indicates that XGBoost is taking on more risk with less reward, as it produces lower returns adjusted for volatility. A similar trend is observed in Gold Futures, where LSTM again leads in Adjusted Total Return (38.77%) compared to XGBoost’s 29.92%, despite both models having the same Mean Return of 0.006. The Return Std. for LSTM in Gold Futures (0.167) is slightly higher than XGBoost’s 0.151, but the increased risk still results in better returns. In Soybean Futures, LSTM produces a much higher Mean Return (0.009) compared to XGBoost’s 0.004, and also delivers higher Adjusted Total Return (39.45% vs. 16.45%), reflecting its ability to generate superior profits even while managing volatility with a Return Std. of 0.208, higher than XGBoost’s 0.204.

For Silver Futures, the results are different. Despite LSTM’s higher Mean Return (0.002 vs. 0.001), the Return Std. for both models is relatively high (0.191 for LSTM and 0.201 for XGBoost), leading to poor Adjusted Total Return for both. LSTM’s Adjusted Total Return of -10.2% contrasts with XGBoost’s -18.11%, indicating that, although LSTM is somewhat better, both models struggle in this volatile market. In Rebar Futures, LSTM again shows better performance, with a Mean Return of 0.009 and Adjusted Total Return of 38.33%, compared to XGBoost’s 0.003 and 15.08%. The Return Std. for both models is relatively low (0.168 for LSTM vs. 0.158 for XGBoost), but LSTM still manages to generate superior returns, showing that it handles the lower-risk environment of Rebar Futures more effectively.

In the 5-minute frequency predictions, the gap in performance between LSTM and XGBoost persists, with LSTM consistently producing higher Adjusted Total Return across all markets except Silver. For Crude Oil Futures, LSTM’s Adjusted Total Return is 37.69%, significantly better than XGBoost’s 26.03%. While XGBoost has a slightly higher Return Std. (0.197), the higher volatility does not yield commensurate returns. LSTM’s ability to generate more substantial returns while maintaining a relatively lower Return Std. (0.181) emphasizes its efficiency at managing risk over this prediction horizon. A similar pattern holds for Gold Futures, where LSTM produces a higher Adjusted Total Return (35.62%) compared to XGBoost’s 28.23%, with Return Std. values of 0.182 and 0.172, respectively.

In Silver Futures, however, XGBoost’s performance is less volatile but still generates poorer returns. The Adjusted Total Return for LSTM is 33.12%, a marked improvement over XGBoost’s negative Adjusted Total Return of -4.90%, which underscores LSTM’s ability to manage risk and volatility better in this market. In Soybean Futures, LSTM’s Adjusted Total Return is again much higher (7.62% vs. 0.53%) than XGBoost’s, and its higher Return Std. (0.247) reflects the greater volatility of this agricultural commodity market, which LSTM handles more effectively than XGBoost. For Rebar Futures, LSTM’s performance is again superior, with an Adjusted Total Return of 10.2% compared to XGBoost’s 1.26%, even with a similar Return Std. (0.186 for LSTM vs. 0.171 for XGBoost).

Finally, at the 15-minute frequency, the performance gap continues to widen in favor of LSTM. LSTM’s ability to generate higher Adjusted Total Return at longer time horizons is especially evident in Crude Oil Futures, where it achieves an Adjusted Total Return of 33.69%, compared to XGBoost’s 15.25%. The Return Std. for LSTM (0.179) is only slightly lower than XGBoost’s (0.188), but it still yields much higher returns. A similar trend occurs in Gold Futures, with LSTM leading with a Total Return of 34.72% compared to XGBoost’s 26.01%, and higher Adjusted Total Return figures, reflecting its better ability to navigate the risks inherent in longer-term predictions.

In Silver Futures, LSTM continues to lead in terms of Adjusted Total Return (31.12%) compared to XGBoost’s 5.90%, showing that, even with higher volatility, LSTM manages to capture greater returns. Soybean Futures and Rebar Futures both show much lower returns across both models, but LSTM still produces better Adjusted Total Return (5.2% vs. -2.02% for Soybean and 0.22% vs. 0.00% for Rebar), underlining its stronger risk-adjusted performance across all timeframes.

Overall, LSTM consistently outperforms XGBoost in terms of Adjusted Total Return, particularly when risk is considered through the Return Std. Both models show a tendency for higher volatility at longer prediction horizons, but LSTM continues to manage that volatility more effectively, yielding higher returns across all markets, even in more volatile futures like Crude Oil and Silver. In contrast, XGBoost, despite showing some competitive performance in certain markets like Soybean Futures, generally fails to produce risk-adjusted returns that are as strong as LSTM’s, especially in more unpredictable markets.

#### 7.3 Features Importance

Feature importance provides insight into which input variables most influence a model’s classification decisions, and this can have direct implications for model interpretability and decision-making. The methods used to assess feature importance, however, vary significantly between LSTM and XGBoost classifiers. The fundamental difference lies in the interpretability and ease of access. XGBoost provides clear, quantifiable importance metrics based on tree splitting and performance gains, making it relatively simple to understand which features drive model predictions. In contrast, LSTM’s feature importance is less transparent due to the model’s architecture, which relies on the temporal relationships between features and requires additional techniques to interpret feature contributions.

In XGBoost, feature importance is directly accessible and interpretable through built-in methods that quantify the contribution of each feature to the model’s predictions. XGBoost uses decision trees as its base learners, and as a result, it is able to compute feature importance by evaluating how frequently a feature is used for splitting nodes in the trees. The two most common approaches to assessing feature importance in XGBoost are:

*   • Weight\-Based Importance: This method counts how often a feature is used to split the data at each node. Features that are used more frequently for splitting are deemed more important. This provides a simple, intuitive way to evaluate feature relevance ([Chen & Guestrin, 2016](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor866)).
    
*   • Gain\-Based Importance: This method measures the improvement in the model’s performance (typically measured by a reduction in loss function) that results from a feature being used in a split. Features that provide the greatest improvement in model accuracy or performance are assigned higher importance. This method captures the contribution of each feature in a more granular way, considering the actual impact of the feature on the model's predictions ([Chen & Guestrin, 2016](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor866)).
    

In the context of this study, where interactive effects between features are expected, F-score by gain is generally the more appropriate measure of feature importance. This is because F-score by gain reflects how much a feature contributes to improving the model’s performance, even if that improvement occurs only when the feature interacts with other features. This is particularly valuable, as feature importance is not solely determined by how frequently a feature is used (as in F-score by weight), but by how much it enhances the model’s predictive accuracy. [Figure 1](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor862) presents an example of a feature importance (by gain) plot for the 1-minute ahead prediction of the gold futures market, generated using the XGBoost package. The F\-scores highlight that past price, volatility, and changes in open interest positions are among the most important features for predicting the direction of futures prices according to the XGBoost classifier. Contrary to anecdotal insights, some technical features employed by the models appear to be insignificant in predicting futures price movements.

#### Figure 1. Feature importance by gain: XGBoost classifier for 1-minute ahead prediction in the gold futures market

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.f01](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.f01.png)

In contrast, LSTM, a type of recurrent neural network (RNN), handles sequential data and temporal dependencies, making it inherently more complex to interpret when it comes to feature importance. LSTM does not provide built-in feature importance measures as easily accessible as those in XGBoost. Since LSTM is a deep learning model, it learns the temporal relationships between features through a series of weighted connections across time steps. The feature importance in LSTM is implicit in the learned weights of the network rather than explicitly defined by feature usage or gain.

However, there are indirect methods to assess feature importance in LSTM models:

*   • Permutation Importance: This method involves perturbing each feature in the input data (for example, by randomly shuffling its values) and observing the change in the model's performance. Features whose perturbation leads to the largest decrease in model accuracy can be considered the most important. This approach can be applied to any model, including LSTM, to estimate the effect of each feature on the model’s predictive power ([Fisher et al., 2019](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor872)).
    
*   • Gradient\-Based Methods: Techniques like saliency maps and Integrated Gradients can be used to analyze the gradients of the loss function with respect to the input features. These methods provide a way to assess which features contribute most to the model’s output at each time step by examining how changes in the feature values affect the model's loss. In the context of LSTM, these methods help identify the most influential features in time-dependent predictions (Simonyan et al., 2013; [Bach et al., 2015](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor864)).
    
*   • Attention Mechanisms: In some LSTM variants, such as Attention-based LSTM models, the model explicitly learns to “attend” to specific parts of the input sequence, giving more weight to certain features or time steps in making predictions. The attention weights can be interpreted as a form of feature importance, highlighting which parts of the input data the model considers most relevant for making its predictions. This approach is particularly useful in sequential tasks like time-series forecasting, where the relative importance of features may vary across time ([Niu et al., 2021](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch014.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor885)).
    

While these techniques provide useful insights, they are generally more computationally intensive and less straightforward than the feature importance metrics available in XGBoost. The interpretability of LSTM models is an ongoing area of research, and while methods like permutation importance and saliency maps can provide valuable insights, they require additional steps and do not offer the same level of transparency that comes with tree-based models like XGBoost.

### 8\. CONCLUSION

This study contributes to the literature on short-term futures market prediction by comparing the performance of two widely used machine learning classifiers—XGBoost and LSTM—in predicting very short-term market direction (1-15 minute horizon). The study focuses on high-frequency trading data from five key Chinese futures markets—Crude Oil, Gold, Soybean, Silver, and Rebar Futures. By evaluating the relative strengths of XGBoost and LSTM, this research fills a significant gap in the literature, as most prior studies have focused on longer-term predictions or price forecasting, rather than very short-term directional forecasting. LSTM, known for capturing sequential dependencies and long\-term patterns in time-series data, and XGBoost, which excels at modeling non-linear relationships within structured datasets, were chosen for their complementary strengths.

The results of this study show that LSTM outperforms XGBoost in terms of prediction accuracy and risk-adjusted returns, especially in volatile markets like Crude Oil and Silver Futures. In contrast, XGBoost performs better in more stable markets such as Soybean and Rebar Futures, where its ability to handle structured data and capture interactions between market features leads to higher stability and efficiency. This comparative analysis provides valuable insights into how these classifiers can be leveraged for short-term directional predictions in high-frequency trading scenarios.

The backtesting results further support the practical implications of this study, as they suggest that both classifiers can generate high-quality trading signals in real-time, high-frequency trading environments. By focusing on the 1\-15 minute prediction horizon, the study demonstrates that both LSTM and XGBoost can provide actionable insights for traders looking to capitalize on short-term market movements. These models are particularly effective at generating timely, reliable predictions in volatile markets, where small, rapid price changes present significant opportunities for high-frequency traders. The study also highlights the potential for combining machine learning classifiers with technical indicators to improve prediction accuracy in real-time trading, reinforcing the practical value of these methods in decision-making processes.

Ultimately, the findings of this study suggest that both LSTM and XGBoost classifiers are promising tools for short\-term futures market prediction, offering distinct advantages depending on the market conditions. By comparing their performance, this research adds to the growing body of knowledge on machine learning applications in financial forecasting, with a specific focus on the unique dynamics of the Chinese futures market. The study's contribution lies not only in its comparative analysis of these two models but also in its exploration of their potential for generating effective trading signals in high-frequency environments, providing valuable insights for both researchers and practitioners in the field of financial forecasting.
