### ABSTRACT

This paper investigates the volatility transmission between the S&P/TSX and key global financial markets, including the S&P500, Gold, VIX, WTI, and Brent Crude Oil (BO), using the Dynamic Correlation-Multivariate Stochastic Volatility (DC-MSV) model. By analyzing daily market index returns, the study uncovers dynamic volatility interactions and spillovers, providing valuable insights into how shocks in one market can affect others. The findings reveal significant bidirectional volatility transmission between the S&P/TSX and S&P500, with notable unidirectional spillovers to Gold and WTI. The results have important implications for financial professionals, especially in Canada, where market volatility and global economic dynamics directly impact investment strategies and risk management. This paper contributes to the literature by offering a comprehensive understanding of volatility transmission across diverse markets and its relevance for portfolio diversification, economic forecasting, and policy formulation.

### 1\. INTRODUCTION

Volatility transmission refers to the process by which volatility shocks in one financial market affect the volatility of other interconnected markets. This phenomenon arises due to various economic, geopolitical, and investor sentiment factors that link markets across borders. For instance, a sudden shock in the volatility of one market, such as a large drop in equity prices or a surge in commodity prices, may trigger similar fluctuations in other markets, either directly or through indirect channels. Understanding volatility transmission is critical for risk management, as it enables investors and financial professionals to gauge the extent to which market fluctuations can propagate across different asset classes, influencing their portfolios. Studying these transmission effects helps in identifying potential vulnerabilities in the global financial system and provides a more comprehensive picture of market risk, especially in times of heightened uncertainty or crisis.

From a Canadian perspective, analyzing the volatility transmission between the S&P/TSX and key global market indices, including the S&P500, Gold, WTI, VIX, and BO, is particularly relevant. The Canadian market is highly integrated into the global economy, with significant exposure to global commodity prices, particularly oil, and other resources. As such, fluctuations in global markets often have a substantial impact on the performance of the S&P/TSX index, which is heavily weighted toward energy and natural resources stocks. Moreover, Canada’s relatively smaller market size compared to larger global economies, such as the U.S. or the Eurozone, makes it more susceptible to external shocks, which can lead to volatility spillovers from global markets. By understanding how volatility in global markets, such as the S&P500 or Gold, affects the Canadian market, financial professionals can better anticipate risks, optimize portfolio allocations, and improve asset diversification strategies.

This paper seeks to deepen the understanding of these interrelationships by modeling the volatility transmission between the S&P/TSX and the other major indices, using a Dynamic Correlation Multivariate Stochastic Volatility (DC-MSV) model. This model is particularly valuable as it accounts for the time-varying nature of volatility and allows for a detailed examination of how volatility propagates across multiple markets. By employing this methodology, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the correlation dynamics between the S&P/TSX and other global financial markets, using daily market index returns over a defined period. The study’s results offer crucial insights into the direction and magnitude of volatility spillovers, shedding light on how shocks in the S&P/TSX index influence other markets and vice versa. These findings are particularly important for Canadian financial professionals, as they can inform strategies for risk management, portfolio construction, and market timing in an increasingly interconnected financial landscape.

The key findings of the study reveal that the S&P/TSX index exhibits the strongest volatility transmission to Gold, a traditionally safe-haven asset, with a significant effect. This suggests that in times of market stress, Canadian investors may look to Gold as a hedge against volatility in the domestic equity market. Additionally, volatility transmission is observed to be bidirectional between the S&P/TSX and other major indices such as the S&P500, highlighting the interconnected nature of these markets. Interestingly, the study also shows that the volatility transmission from S&P/TSX to WTI and to BO (oil prices) is notable, which underscores the critical role of energy prices in shaping market sentiment in Canada. While the Canadian market appears to be significantly affected by the VIX, it does not transfer volatility to the VIX to the same extent. These results not only offer valuable insights into the specific dynamics of the S&P/TSX but also contribute to the broader understanding of how Canadian markets interact with key global financial indicators.

The rest of this article is organized as follows: In Section 2, the Literature Review provides an overview of the existing studies related to volatility transmission between oil prices, stock market indices, and other financial assets, highlighting the key methodologies and findings in the field. Section 3, the Overview of the Financial Markets, introduces the key financial markets examined in this study, including the S&P/TSX, S&P500, Gold, VIX, Brent Crude Oil (BO), and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil, with an emphasis on their characteristics and relevance to the study of volatility transmission. In Section 4, the Methodology section outlines the Multivariate Stochastic Volatility (DC-MSV) model employed to analyze the dynamic volatility interactions among these markets. Section 5, titled Data and Findings, presents the empirical results of the volatility transmission analysis, providing detailed insights into the relationships and time-varying volatility spillovers between the markets. Section 6, Implications, discusses the practical applications of these findings for financial professionals, investors, and policymakers, particularly those in Canada, and highlights how understanding volatility transmission can inform risk management strategies and investment decisions. Finally, Section 7, the Conclusion, summarizes the main findings, discusses the limitations of the study, and proposes directions for future research.

### 2\. LITERATURE REVIEW

The relationship between oil prices, the Volatility Index (VIX), and various stock market indices has been widely studied in the financial literature using a variety of methodologies. However, there is a limited body of research that employs the Multivariate Stochastic Volatility (DC-MSV) model, particularly in the context of volatility transmission between different markets. This section reviews key studies that explore volatility spillovers between oil markets, equity indices, and other financial assets, highlighting the gap in literature that this study aims to fill.

[Hepsağ (2013)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor935) examined the volatility interactions between Brent Crude Oil (BO) prices and industrial sector indices of MIST countries (Mexico, Indonesia, South Korea, and Turkey). Using several models, including the CCC-GARCH, DCC-GARCH, CCC-MSV, and DCC-MSV, the study concluded that there is a time-varying correlation between industrial sector returns and crude oil returns across all countries. These correlations were found to change over time, reflecting the dynamic nature of the relationship between oil prices and stock market returns. This finding suggests that volatility spillovers are not static and are influenced by various macroeconomic and geopolitical factors.

[Kılıç (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor938) employed the DC-MSV model to analyze the stochastic volatility spillovers between oil risk, the oil spot market, and oil futures markets. The study found no significant volatility transmission between oil risk and the oil spot market, but revealed a positive bidirectional volatility spillover between oil risk and the oil futures market. Additionally, the research identified a unidirectional volatility transmission from the oil spot market to the oil futures market. These findings emphasize the importance of the futures market in transmitting volatility, highlighting its role as a key channel through which oil market risk spreads across different segments of the financial system.

[Le et al. (2022)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor939) applied a time-varying parameter vector autoregression model with stochastic volatility (TVP-VAR-SV) to investigate the factors influencing the realized volatility of WTI crude oil prices. The study found that WTI volatility responded positively to factors such as oil production, oil inventories, the US dollar index, and the VIX, with the VIX having the most significant impact. The analysis also showed that the volatility response of WTI prices was particularly pronounced during periods of economic crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, underscoring the sensitivity of oil markets to both economic shocks and financial market conditions.

Vo (2011) explored the volatility interactions between the oil market and the S&P500 index using both the CCC-MSV and DCC-MSV models. The study found a strong and significant volatility relationship between the oil market and the S&P500, suggesting that fluctuations in oil prices have a substantial impact on stock market volatility, and vice versa. This highlights the interconnectedness of commodity markets and equity markets, with volatility in one market often spilling over into the other, particularly during periods of heightened market uncertainty.

Building on these foundational studies, the current article contributes to the literature by examining the volatility transmission between the S&P/TSX Composite Index, S&P500, Gold, VIX, Brent Crude Oil (BO), and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) Oil using the DC-MSV model. By focusing on the dynamic, time-varying relationships between these markets, this study provides detailed insights into how shocks in one market affect the volatility of others. In particular, the study aims to shed light on the volatility spillover effects between the Canadian market (S&P/TSX) and other global financial and commodity markets. The results offer up-to-date and comprehensive information on the volatility transmission between these markets, providing valuable insights for both academic research and practical applications in risk management and financial decision-making.

This paper not only addresses a gap in the literature by applying the DC-MSV model to a broad set of financial data but also provides critical implications for Canadian financial professionals. The findings offer a better understanding of how global market dynamics influence Canadian market volatility, with particular focus on how the Canadian stock market interacts with global oil prices, U.S. equity markets, and the VIX. By enhancing our understanding of these volatility transmission mechanisms, the study helps financial analysts, investors, and policymakers in making more informed decisions in an increasingly interconnected global financial landscape.

### 3\. OVERVIEW OF THE FINANCIAL MARKETS

This study focuses on analyzing the volatility transmission between several key financial markets, specifically the S&P/TSX Composite Index, the S&P500, Brent Crude Oil (BO), West Texas Intermediate (WTI) Oil, the VIX (Volatility Index), and Gold. Each of these markets plays a crucial role in the global financial system, and understanding the interactions between them provides valuable insights into risk management and market dynamics, especially from the perspective of Canadian financial professionals.

The S&P/TSX Composite Index represents the largest companies in Canada, providing a comprehensive overview of the Canadian stock market and serving as a barometer for the health of the Canadian economy. This index is heavily weighted toward the energy sector, which makes it particularly sensitive to fluctuations in global energy prices, including the prices of oil. The S&P500, one of the most well-known indices in the United States, tracks the performance of 500 of the largest publicly traded companies in the U.S. This index spans a wide range of sectors, including technology, energy, healthcare, and finance, and is highly correlated with the S&P/TSX, reflecting shared economic trends but also differences in sectoral composition. The volatility of these two indices is particularly important for Canadian investors as they are often used as benchmarks for global economic conditions and for understanding the impact of U.S. market movements on Canadian assets.

In addition to these stock indices, this study also examines Brent Crude (BO) and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) Oil, which are two of the most influential benchmark crude oils globally. BO is primarily extracted from the North Sea and is favored for its lower refining costs and easier transportation by sea, making it a preferred choice for international markets. WTI, extracted in the United States, is typically refined into gasoline and other light products and is used as the primary oil benchmark for the U.S. market. The prices of these oil benchmarks are key drivers of global economic conditions, influencing everything from inflation to energy policies.

Another critical market factor analyzed in this study is the VIX, or Volatility Index, often referred to as the “fear index.” The VIX measures market uncertainty and investor sentiment by tracking implied volatility of options on the S&P500. It serves as a key indicator of market risk and investor anxiety, rising during periods of financial instability or economic crises. Lastly, Gold is included in this study due to its role as a safe-haven asset. Investors often turn to Gold during periods of heightened market risk or economic uncertainty, making it an important asset for understanding the dynamics of volatility transmission across markets.

Together, these markets—S&P/TSX, S&P500, Brent Crude, WTI, the VIX, and Gold—offer a broad view of global financial trends and risk factors. By examining the volatility transmission between these markets, this study provides insights into how shocks or price fluctuations in one market can ripple through to others, affecting everything from investment strategies to risk management.

The analysis presented in this paper is particularly relevant for Canadian financial professionals. Canada’s economy is heavily reliant on the energy sector, particularly oil, and understanding how global energy markets and key global indices like the S&P500 affect the S&P/TSX can offer valuable insights into market dynamics. Given the high correlation between Canadian and U.S. markets, as well as the significant influence of global oil prices on Canada’s economic performance, understanding volatility transmission between these markets can help Canadian investors and financial analysts anticipate market movements, manage risk, and make more informed investment decisions.

### 4\. METHODOLOGY

This section introduces the volatility forecasting models and machine learning techniques utilized to achieve the results of this study.

#### 4.1 Overview of Volatility Models

##### 4.1.1 ARCH and GARCH Models

ARCH (Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity) and GARCH (Generalized ARCH) models are commonly used for volatility forecasting, focusing on modeling time-varying conditional variance. These models are symmetric, assuming that positive and negative shocks affect volatility in the same way. The ARCH model, developed by [Engle (1982)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor933), introduced the concept of time-varying conditional variance, in contrast to earlier models that assumed constant variance over time. The GARCH model, introduced by [Bollerslev (1986)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor931), extends ARCH by incorporating both past error terms and past conditional variances to model volatility more comprehensively.

Despite their widespread use, ARCH and GARCH models are limited by their symmetry, meaning they cannot capture the leverage effect, where negative shocks tend to have a stronger impact on volatility than positive shocks. To address this, models like EGARCH ([Nelson, 1991](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor940)) and TGARCH ([Zakoian, 1994](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor944)) were developed to allow for asymmetric effects, offering a better fit for financial volatility ([Güriş, 2020](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor934)).

##### 4.1.2 Stochastic Volatility Models

Stochastic volatility (SV) models, introduced by Taylor (1986), provide an alternative to ARCH-type models by treating volatility as an unobservable latent variable. This latent process allows SV models to capture more complex volatility patterns compared to the deterministic assumptions in ARCH-type models. By modeling both the conditional and unconditional features of volatility, SV models offer greater flexibility and power in forecasting financial asset volatility ([Broto and Ruiz, 2004](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor932)). Unlike ARCH-type models that primarily focus on conditional volatility, SV models can incorporate both short-term and long-term volatility dynamics ([Hepsağ, 2013](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor935)).

###### 4.1.2.1 Basic Stochastic Volatility (SV) Model for Single Asset Returns

The basic Stochastic Volatility (SV) model for a single asset return is given by:

  
$$y\_{t} = {e^{\\frac{h\_{t}}{2}}\\epsilon\_{t}}$$  
(1)

Where:

*   • y[t] is the observed return of the asset at time t,
    
*   • h[t] is the latent (unobserved) volatility at time t, and exp(h[t]/2) ensures that the volatility is strictly positive (as the volatility must be positive).
    
*   • *ϵ*[*t*] is the standard normal innovation (i.e., the shock or error term)
    

The volatility hth\_tht itself follows a first\-order autoregressive process (AR(1)), which models the evolution of the log-volatility over time. This can be written as:

  
*h*[*t*] = *γ* + *ϕ**h*[*t* − 1] + *η*[*t*]  
(2)

where:

*   • γ is a constant term (often set to 0 for simplicity),
    
*   • ϕ is the persistence parameter, which determines how much past volatility affects current volatility,
    
*   • η[t] is the innovation or shock to volatility, which is assumed to follow a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance σ2.
    

###### 4.1.2.2 Multivariate Stochastic Volatility (MSV) Model

The SV model can be extended to the Multivariate Stochastic Volatility (MSV) model by considering the returns of nnn assets at time t, denoted as y[t]\= (*y*[1, *t*], *y*[2, *t*],...... *y*[*n*, *t*]) and a vector of latent volatilities h[t]\=(*h*[1, *t*], *h*[2, *t*],…, *h*[*n*, *t*]), where each *h*[*i*, *t*] follows an independent AR(1) process. For simplicity, this study focuses on the bivariate case where n=2. In this case, the model is represented as:

*y*[*t*] = *Ω*[*t*]*ϵ*[*t*]

Where:

*   • $\\Omega\_{t} = diag~\\left( e^{\\frac{h\_{t}}{2}} \\right)$
    
*   • $\\epsilon\_{t}\\overset{iid}{\\sim}N\\left( {0,I} \\right)$
    

The volatility process evolves according to:

*h*[*t* + 1]\=*μ*+*d**i**a**g*( *ϕ*[11] , *ϕ*[22])(*h*[*t*]−*μ*) + *η*[*t*]

Where:

*   • μ=h[0] (the initial volatility)
    
*   • $\\eta\_{t}\\overset{iid}{\\sim}N\\left( {0,diag\\left( \\sigma\_{\\eta\_{1}}^{2},\\sigma\_{\\eta\_{2}}^{2} \\right)} \\right)$
    

This model is essentially a combination of two univariate SV models, capturing leptokurtic return distributions and volatility clustering. However, it does not account for correlations or Granger causality between returns or volatilities.

###### 4.1.2.3 Dynamic Correlation Multivariate Stochastic Volatility (DC\-MSV) Model

A more advanced bivariate model is the DC-MSV model introduced by [Yu and Meyer (2006)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor943), which allows for time-varying correlations and volatilities. The model can be expressed as:

*y*[*t*] = *Ω*[*t*]*ϵ*[*t*],

Where Ω[t] is a diagonal matrix containing time-varying volatilities (as defined in equation (3)), and ϵ[t] is the shock vector at time t, assumed to follow an iid normal distribution with zero mean and a time-varying covariance matrix *Σ*[*ϵ*, *t*] with correlation *ρ*[*t*] bounded between -1 and +1:

$\\Sigma\_{\\epsilon,t} = \\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \\rho\_{t} \\\\ \\rho\_{t} & 1 \\\\ \\end{pmatrix}$

The time-varying volatilities evolve according to:

*h*[*t* + 1]\=*μ*+*d**i**a**g*( *ϕ*[11] , *ϕ*[22])(*h*[*t*]−*μ*) + *η*[*t*]

Where,

*   • $\\eta\_{t}\\overset{iid}{\\sim}N\\left( {0,diag\\left( \\sigma\_{\\eta\_{1}}^{2},\\sigma\_{\\eta\_{2}}^{2} \\right)} \\right)$
    
*   • μ=h[0]
    

Additionally, the process for the correlation *ρ*[*t*] is given by:

$q\_{0} = \\psi\_{0},~q\_{t + 1} = \\psi\_{0} + ~\\psi\\left( {q\_{t} - \\psi\_{0}~} \\right) + ~\\sigma\_{p}~\\nu\_{t},~\\nu\_{t}\\overset{iid}{\\sim}N\\left( 0,1 \\right)$

Where 𝜌[t] is determined as: ![](image/2.png)

In this model:

*   • η[t] and *ϵ*[*t*] are independent random variables with homogeneous distribution
    
*   • ϕ measures the stability of shocks to volatility.
    
*   • h[t] represents unobservable volatility.
    
*   • *σ*[*η*]² is the variance of the volatility process, indicating uncertainty about future volatility.
    

There is an inverse relationship between *σ*[*η*]², and ϕ, with *σ*[*η*]², approaching zero as ϕ approaches 1 ([Yu and Meyer, 2006](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor943)).

### 5\. DATA AND FINDINGS

In this study, daily data obtained from the “Yahoo Finance” database between 01.01.2016 and 25.10.2024 were used. The study investigates the volatility transmission mechanism between S&P/TSX and S&P500, Gold, VIX, BO, and WTI. The abbreviations used in the study are as follows: S&P/TSX refers to the Toronto Stock Exchange composite index, BO represents Brent Oil, VIX is the Fear Index, and WTI denotes West Texas Intermediate. The DC-MSV model was employed as the research method, which assumes that correlation coefficients and volatilities change over time. To optimize the model and ensure accurate parameter estimation, 50,000 iterations were performed for each model. The iterations are essential in this process as they allow the model to gradually refine its parameter estimates. Each iteration involves adjusting the model’s parameters based on the errors from the previous step, leading to convergence toward an optimal solution. This iterative process ensures that the model captures the time-varying nature of volatility transmission and improves its forecasting accuracy.

#### 5.1 Descriptive Statistics and Prelimitary Analysis

The time path graph of the variables considered in the study for the period from January 2016 to October 2024 is shown in [Figure 1](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor919). The variables generally exhibited an irregular trajectory, with notable fluctuations occurring during the pandemic period.

#### Figure 1. Changes in S&P/TSX, S&P500, gold, VIX, WTI, and BO series

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f01](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f01.png)

Return series are calculated for all variables using the formula ![](image/3.png) The periodic changes of the return series are shown in [Figure 2](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor920).

Upon examining the graphs, it is evident that there are numerous extreme values. The presence of these extreme values suggests volatility clustering, which indicates serial dependence within the time series data ([Khofifahturizqi et al., 2024](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor937)).

When analyzing the graphs of the variables in [Figure 2](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor920), it is clear that there were significant volatile movements during the pandemic period. Additionally, between 2022 and 2023, the volatility of these variables increased once again, driven by factors such as the Russia-Ukraine War, the global energy crisis, economic uncertainty, and supply chain disruptions.

The most significant decline in oil prices since World War II occurred between 2014 and 2016. Contributing factors included the rising shale gas production in the US, increased productivity in the oil sector, and deteriorating demand expectations ([Stocker et al., 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor941)). The uncertainty surrounding the US elections during this period also led to heightened market volatility. For instance, a 4% drop in the S&P 500 index in February 2018 resulted in a 20-point surge in the volatility of the VIX. The rapid liquidation of high-volatility investment products (ETPs) and a shift to low-volatility products contributed to this surge, causing the VIX to spike sharply ([Sushko & Turner, 2018](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor942)). These events explain the sudden fluctuations observed in the VIX during 2018 in [Figure 2](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor920).

#### Figure 2. Change in S&P/TSX, S&P500, gold, VIX, WTI, and BO volatilities

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f02](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f02.png)

#### Figure 3. Correlation matrix between S&P/TSX and S&P500, GOLD, VIX, WTI, and BO

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f03](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f03.png)

[Figure 3](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor921) shows the correlation matrix between S&P/TSX and the rest of the index returns. The correlation matrix shows the direction and strength of the relationship between variables in a dataset. In particular, it assesses the linear relationship of each variable with the others. A correlation coefficient of 0 indicates that there is no relationship between two variables. As we move from 0 to 1 or -1, the strength of the relationship increases. A correlation coefficient of 1 indicates a perfect positive correlation between two variables, while -1 means the existence of a perfect negative correlation between two variables.

The variable with the strongest correlation to S&P/TSX is the S&P500 index (0.82), followed by BO (0.38). GOLD exhibits the weakest correlation with S&P/TSX. Another interesting finding is the correlation between VIX and other variables. VIX has a negative correlation with BO, WTI, S&P/TSX, and S&P500, but a positive correlation with GOLD. A negative correlation typically suggests that as market uncertainty (indicated by rising VIX) increases, stock values decline, and economic growth expectations fall, which in turn negatively impacts oil demand. The positive correlation between VIX and GOLD can be explained by investors seeking safer assets, like gold, during uncertain times. Gold tends to appreciate during economic downturns, making it a preferred asset when markets face heightened uncertainty.

Examining the change in the correlation between variables over time is important when making investment decisions. The 6-month lagged time-dependent correlation change is shown in [Figure 4](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor922). The reason for performing the correlation analysis with a 6-month lag is that it allows capturing periodic fluctuations. This type of analysis is useful to provide better foresight when making investment decisions. Daily correlations are easily affected by market volatility and price movements. Therefore, in order to reduce this noise, periodic correlation analysis was deemed appropriate. [Figure 4](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor922) shows how the relationship between S&P/TSX and other assets has changed over time.

#### Figure 4. Dynamic correlation matrix between S&P/TSX and S&P500, GOLD, VIX, WTI, and BO

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f04](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f04.png)

When the time-dependent correlation of S&P/TSX with other variables is analyzed, it is seen that the correlation relationship is relatively stable in the 2020-2021 period. The economic recession and supply chain disruptions following the pandemic caused uncertainty in stock markets and commodity markets. This situation created similar patterns among the variables and caused the correlation relationship to remain the same. In 2022, the sudden outbreak of the Russian-Ukrainian war caused the VIX to gain upward momentum and energy prices to skyrocket. This led to an increase in the correlation between the S&P/TSX, energy assets and the VIX. Another point is that the correlation between the S&P/TSX and the S&P500 indices remained relatively stable yet strong throughout the period analyzed.

\* indicates statistical significance at 5% significance level.

Upon analyzing the descriptive statistics of the variables, it is observed that the average returns of all variables, except WTI, are slightly above zero. A positive average return suggests that, over time, the financial assets have generally performed favorably, with the potential for generating positive returns for investors. In contrast, the negative average return of WTI indicates a decline over the period under review. The fact that the mean values of the returns are smaller than the standard deviation values suggests that the series follow a random walk, which is characteristic of many financial time series.

For a normal distribution, the kurtosis value is 3, referred to as mesokurtic, while a distribution with a kurtosis value greater than 3 is considered leptokurtic ([Akinlawon et al., 2010](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor930)). Financial data typically exhibit leptokurtic distributions. The kurtosis values reported in [Table 1](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor923) confirm that the series are leptokurtic, with thick tails. Additionally, the Jarque-Bera (JB) test statistics indicate that none of the series follow a normal distribution.

One of the fundamental assumptions in econometrics is that error terms are normally distributed. According to the central limit theorem, as the sample size increases, the sample distribution approaches normality. Therefore, the assumption of normality becomes particularly important when working with small sample sizes. When error terms are not normally distributed, the results of statistical tests may be misleading. In financial series, normal distributions are rare, and the skewness and kurtosis values often deviate from normality. The non-normal distribution of error terms can lead to biased test statistics and unreliable results.

Tests such as the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test and Phillips-Perron test are based on the assumption of normality, and their critical values are derived within this framework. Lee, and Tieslau (2014) argue that non-normal distributions cannot be ignored in unit root tests and recommend using tests that are appropriate for non-normally distributed series in order to obtain more efficient estimators ([Hepsağ, 2022](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor936)). As shown in [Table 1](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor923), the Jarque-Bera normality test results for the series used in this study indicate that these series are not normally distributed. Therefore, instead of the ADF unit root test, the Rals-LM unit root test was preferred for testing the stationarity of non-normally distributed series.

According to the results of the DC-MSV model for the S&P/TSX and S&P500 variables presented in [Table 2](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor924), the parameter Φ[TSX], which reflects the volatility of the S&P/TSX index returns and the persistence of volatility, is statistically significant at the 5% significance level. The value of this parameter (0.8898) is very close to 1, indicating that the volatility of the index is persistent and exhibits volatility clustering. This suggests that a sudden shock to the S&P/TSX is not absorbed quickly and has a long-lasting effect on the index.

Similarly, the parameter Φ[S&P500], which captures the volatility of the S&P500 index, is also statistically significant, with a value of 0.9220. A parameter value close to 1 implies that volatility in the S&P500 is persistent, and shocks to the index have a lasting impact, consistent with the presence of volatility clusters.

The parameters Φ[S&P500-TSX] and Φ[TSX-S&P500], which represent the effect of volatility transmission between the two indices, are also statistically significant. This suggests that the volatility transmission mechanism between the S&P/TSX and the S&P500 operates in both directions. Specifically, a 1% shock in the S&P500 will increase the volatility of the S&P/TSX by 0.0828% on the following trading day, while a 1% shock in the S&P/TSX will increase the volatility of the S&P500 by 0.0699% on the next trading day. These results indicate that the volatility transmission between the two indices is bidirectional, with the S&P500 having a relatively larger impact on the volatility of the S&P/TSX compared to the reverse effect.

The parameters Ψ[TSX] and Ψ[S&P500], which represent the correlation between the S&P/TSX and S&P500 indices, are statistically significant, indicating a strong and dynamic relationship between these two variables.

The parameters σ[TSX] and σ[S&P500], which measure the predictability of future volatilities for the respective indices, are statistically significant at the 5% significance level. The squared values of these parameters (0.0505 for S&P/TSX and 0.0495 for S&P500) suggest that the volatilities of these two indices are relatively predictable. The closer these squared values are to zero, the more predictable the volatilities of the indices are. Therefore, it can be concluded that the future volatility of the S&P/TSX and S&P500 indices is at a predictable level.

### 6\. IMPLICATIONS

#### Figure 5. Summary of volatility transmission mechanism between S&P/TSX and S&P500, GOLD, VIX, WTI, and BO

![979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f05](image/979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.f05.png)

[Figure 5](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch015.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor929) presents a volatility transmission diagram that summarizes the key findings discussed in this section. The diagram illustrates the direction and strength of volatility transmission among the variables under consideration. The strongest volatility transmission from S&P/TSX was to Gold (0.4919), while the strongest transmission to S&P/TSX was from the S&P500 (0.0828). On the other hand, the weakest volatility transmission from S&P/TSX was to the VIX (0.0050), and the weakest volatility transmission to S&P/TSX was from BO (0.0209). These findings offer valuable insights into the risk dynamics between these financial assets.

The fact that Gold experiences such a strong volatility transmission (0.4919) may be attributed to its status as a safe-haven asset. During periods of market uncertainty or stress, investors often flock to Gold as a store of value, shielding themselves from risks that may affect equities and other commodities. Therefore, shocks to the S&P/TSX index are likely amplified in Gold, as investors use it to hedge against financial market fluctuations.

In contrast, the low volatility transmission from S&P/TSX to VIX (0.0050) suggests that the broader market’s volatility movements are not directly reflected in the volatility index. This could indicate that the S&P/TSX is not as sensitive to short-term fluctuations in investor sentiment, as reflected by the VIX, which typically rises in response to heightened market fears or economic uncertainty. Therefore, despite the general perception that VIX is a barometer for market volatility, the data suggests that S&P/TSX volatility may be driven more by underlying economic factors rather than mere investor sentiment.

The strong bidirectional volatility transmission between the S&P/TSX and the S&P500 further emphasizes the close relationship between these indices. The value of 0.0699 for S&P/TSX’s impact on the S&P500, and 0.0828 for the reverse, indicates that both indices react similarly to global economic conditions, geopolitical events, and changes in investor sentiment. These indices are often driven by similar macroeconomic factors such as interest rates, inflation expectations, and global growth trends. As such, the correlation between these two indices suggests that their risk profiles are aligned, meaning that an investor in one index may experience similar risk exposure to an investor in the other.

Moreover, the bidirectional volatility transmission between the S&P/TSX and the S&P500 provides important implications for portfolio management. Investors seeking diversification benefits should consider the strong interconnectedness between these two indices. Although they are based on different geographic markets (Canada and the U.S.), their similar volatility characteristics suggest that the two indices will likely move in tandem during periods of economic turbulence or global market shocks. As a result, diversification between these two indices might not provide the intended risk reduction during highly volatile periods.

Another important observation is that while significant volatility transmission occurs from S&P/TSX to WTI and BO, there is no volatility transmission from WTI to S&P/TSX and only limited transmission from BO. This suggests that energy prices are significantly influenced by market movements, but the degree of interaction between S&P/TSX and these commodities differs. This finding can offer investors insight into how different commodities react differently to stock market movements, providing a nuanced understanding of the interconnectedness between financial assets.

Overall, these findings underscore the complex nature of market volatility and the various factors that drive it. They highlight the importance of understanding volatility transmission when making investment decisions, as it can provide investors with insights into the dynamic relationships between asset classes, helping them manage risk and optimize their portfolios. This information is vital for designing strategies that account for both short-term and long-term market risk.

### 7\. CONCLUSION

This study has provided a comprehensive analysis of the volatility transmission between the S&P/TSX Composite Index, S&P500, Gold, VIX, and key oil benchmarks such as Brent Crude Oil (BO) and West Texas Intermediate (WTI), using the Multivariate Stochastic Volatility (DC-MSV) model. The results reveal several important dynamics in the interrelationships between these financial and commodity markets, with significant implications for financial professionals, investors, and policymakers, particularly in Canada.

Our findings show that volatility transmission in the Canadian financial market (S&P/TSX) is predominantly influenced by global markets, with a notably strong transmission from the S&P500 and Gold, and weaker, yet significant, spillovers from oil markets, particularly WTI and BO. This suggests that, while the S&P/TSX responds to global market shocks, especially from U.S. equity markets, the volatility interactions between oil prices and Canadian equities, particularly in the energy sector, warrant particular attention. Additionally, the study highlights the dynamic nature of volatility spillovers, indicating that these relationships are not static and can evolve over time based on shifting macroeconomic conditions, geopolitical events, and financial crises.

The analysis of the VIX as a gauge of market fear reveals its significant role in shaping the volatility of broader markets and its strong relationship with the S&P/TSX benchmark. Notably, while the Canadian market is significantly influenced by the volatility of the VIX, it does not affect the VIX's volatility to the same extent. This highlights the need for further research to understand the impact of investor sentiment in different regional markets, particularly during times of crisis or heightened uncertainty.

From a practical perspective, this research offers critical insights for Canadian financial professionals and investors seeking to manage portfolio risk. By understanding the volatility transmission mechanisms between the Canadian stock market and key global markets, stakeholders can better hedge against risks and develop strategies that are resilient to global shocks. For example, investors in the Canadian energy sector might find it beneficial to monitor global oil prices and the S&P500 to anticipate market movements, while also considering the potential impacts of gold as a safe-haven asset.

While this study significantly advances our understanding of volatility transmission across major global financial and commodity markets, there are several avenues for future research. First, the scope of the model could be expanded to include other key commodities, such as natural gas and agricultural products, to further examine how these commodities interact with oil prices and financial markets, particularly in times of market stress. The inclusion of additional markets could provide a more complete picture of global risk transmission and its effects on regional markets.

Second, future studies could explore the role of financial market sentiment in driving volatility transmission. While the VIX was included in this study, it would be interesting to extend this analysis by incorporating sentiment indices, news sentiment analysis, or other investor behavior metrics to capture how psychological factors influence market volatility and spillovers.

Third, examining the role of central banks and monetary policy in shaping volatility transmission could be a promising area for future research. For example, central bank actions such as interest rate changes, quantitative easing, or fiscal stimulus programs can affect the dynamics of market volatility, particularly in interconnected markets like the S&P/TSX and S&P500. Investigating how these policy measures influence volatility transmission could provide more insights for portfolio management, especially in the context of emerging market economies and their interactions with global financial centers.

Moreover, the impact of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors on volatility spillovers could be another relevant avenue for future exploration. As ESG considerations become increasingly important in investment decision-making, understanding how ESG factors influence the volatility transmission between commodity markets and stock indices could help investors better align their portfolios with sustainable and responsible investment goals.

Finally, an interesting direction for further research could involve the application of advanced machine learning techniques to model volatility transmission. While the DC-MSV model provides a robust framework, machine learning models, such as deep learning or reinforcement learning, could be employed to capture non-linear relationships and improve the accuracy of predictions in a rapidly changing market environment.

### ABSTRACT

Natural Language Processing (NLP) has emerged as a transformative force in finance, enabling firms to extract insights from unstructured data sources such as news articles, earnings reports, and social media feeds. This chapter explores the integration of NLP techniques within the financial sector, focusing on foundational methodologies like tokenization, sentiment analysis, and topic modeling. Applications are examined in areas including algorithmic trading, credit risk assessment, and fraud detection. Furthermore, advanced models such as transformers and embeddings are discussed for their potential to enhance financial data analysis. The chapter also addresses challenges and ethical considerations, including data privacy and algorithmic bias. Future research directions are outlined, emphasizing the potential of emerging technologies like reinforcement learning in conjunction with NLP to develop more robust financial models. This comprehensive overview aims to equip researchers and practitioners with essential knowledge to leverage NLP techniques for strategic advantage in finance.

### 1\. INTRODUCTION

Natural Language Processing (NLP) has rapidly evolved into a cornerstone of technological innovation in the finance sector, fundamentally altering how financial institutions leverage unstructured text data for strategic decision-making. As organizations face an ever-growing influx of information—from news articles and earnings reports to social media and regulatory filings—the ability to efficiently process and analyze this data has become imperative. The integration of NLP techniques enables financial professionals to uncover insights that were previously difficult to access, thereby enhancing trading strategies, improving risk assessment, and bolstering customer engagement.

A 2016 study by Donelson, McInnis, and Mergenthaler explores the factors contributing to the rules-based characteristics of U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). The authors identify and test five key theories: litigation risk, constraining opportunism, complexity, transaction frequency, and age. Their findings suggest that litigation risk and complexity are the most consistent factors associated with rules-based features in accounting standards. While transaction frequency, the age of standards, and efforts to limit opportunistic reporting by regulators show limited relevance, complexity and litigation risk emerge as the most significant influences. However, the study emphasizes that due to the endogenous nature of accounting standards and the interrelated complexity of both the standards and underlying transactions, the results should be interpreted as descriptive rather than causal ([Donelson, McInnis, & Mergenthaler, 2016](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch016.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor974)).

NLP techniques such as sentiment analysis, topic modeling, named entity recognition, and text summarization are increasingly employed to navigate the complexities of the financial landscape. By analyzing sentiment from financial news and reports, traders can better gauge market sentiment, leading to more informed trading decisions. Furthermore, NLP plays a pivotal role in fraud detection and compliance monitoring, enabling institutions to meet regulatory demands while minimizing risks.

As NLP continues to evolve, Generative AI has emerged as a revolutionary extension of these technologies. While traditional NLP techniques focus on processing and analyzing existing text, Generative AI pushes the boundaries by enabling machines to create entirely new, coherent content based on patterns learned from data. In the context of finance, this means not just analyzing market sentiment or identifying key trends but also generating new reports, insights, and even predictive models in real time. This shift from analysis to creation is opening up new avenues for financial decision-making, automation, and innovation.

Generative AI leverages advanced machine learning models such as transformers and embeddings—models that are not only capable of analyzing large volumes of text but also creating novel content based on learned patterns.

Unlike traditional AI and machine learning, which focus on predictions and classifications, Generative AI can enhance operational efficiency by generating new and meaningful content, such as market predictions, investment reports, or automated customer support. The transformative potential of this technology is already being felt across industries, with the financial sector being no exception. According to statistics published by MarketResearch.biz, the global generative AI market in financial services is projected to grow from USD 847.2 million in 2022 to approximately USD 9,475.2 million by 2032, at an impressive Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 28.1%.

Financial institutions, such as banks, are increasingly integrating generative AI into their processes to drive innovation, maintain a competitive edge, and shape the future of financial services. For example, according to [Takyar (2024)](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch016.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor995), the CEO of LeewayHertz, generative AI has the potential to fundamentally enhance every aspect of financial operations for banking institutions (see [Figure 1](#979-8-3693-8186-1.ch016.bits-pdf.xhtml#_idTextAnchor965)).

As we delve deeper into the techniques, applications, and emerging trends in NLP and Generative AI within the finance domain, this chapter aims to illuminate the capabilities and implications of these technologies in reshaping financial decision-making processes. Additionally, NLP supports financial knowledge mining and automates literature analysis, driving innovation in investment strategies and financial products.
